Assuming \(M_1\) and \(M_2\) are nMOS devices with their sources and bodies at ground, the important connections are

\[
\begin{array}{c|cc}
& V_{GS} & V_{DS}\\ \hline
M_1 & V_X & V_{\text{out}}\\
M_2 & V_{\text{out}} & V_X
\end{array}
\]

Thus \(M_2\) is not simply in parallel with \(M_1\): its gate is driven by \(V_{\text{out}}\), while its drain is node \(X\). This creates positive feedback.

Let \(R_D=R_{D1}\), \(v_x=V_X\), and \(v_o=V_{\text{out}}\). Neglecting gate currents and any external output load, the DC equations are

\[
I_{\text{in}}=I_{D2}(V_{GS2}=v_o,V_{DS2}=v_x)
\]

and

\[
\frac{V_{DD}-v_o}{R_D}
=
I_{D1}(V_{GS1}=v_x,V_{DS1}=v_o).
\]

These two nonlinear equations determine the possible DC operating points.

## Qualitative operation

For a small positive \(I_{\text{in}}\):

- \(M_2\) is on because its gate is near \(V_{DD}\).
- \(M_2\) sinks the input current, keeping \(V_X\) low.
- \(M_1\) is off or weakly on.
- Therefore \(V_{\text{out}}\approx V_{DD}\).

As \(I_{\text{in}}\) increases:

1. \(V_X\) rises.
2. \(M_1\) turns on harder.
3. \(V_{\text{out}}\) falls.
4. The lower \(V_{\text{out}}\) weakens \(M_2\).
5. A weaker \(M_2\) allows \(V_X\) to rise even more.

Hence the feedback is regenerative:

\[
V_X\uparrow \;\Rightarrow\; V_{\text{out}}\downarrow
\;\Rightarrow\; I_{D2}\downarrow
\;\Rightarrow\; V_X\uparrow .
\]

The circuit is therefore a regenerative threshold element / negative-resistance cell, rather than an ordinary linear current-to-voltage converter.

---

## Small-signal analysis

At a DC bias point, define

\[
G_D=\frac{1}{R_D}+g_{ds1}.
\]

The small-signal node equations are

\[
i_{\text{in}}=g_{ds2}v_x+g_{m2}v_o
\]

and

\[
G_Dv_o+g_{m1}v_x=0.
\]

Solving,

\[
\boxed{
\frac{v_x}{i_{\text{in}}}
=
\frac{G_D}
{G_Dg_{ds2}-g_{m1}g_{m2}}
}
\]

and

\[
\boxed{
\frac{v_o}{i_{\text{in}}}
=
-\frac{g_{m1}}
{G_Dg_{ds2}-g_{m1}g_{m2}}
}
\]

The critical quantity is

\[
\Delta=G_Dg_{ds2}-g_{m1}g_{m2}.
\]

- If \(\Delta>0\), the operating point is locally nonregenerative.
- If \(\Delta=0\), the small-signal gain becomes very large; this is the switching or fold point.
- If \(\Delta<0\), the input node has negative incremental resistance and the circuit is regenerative/unstable in the linear sense.

The input resistance seen at \(X\) is

\[
\boxed{
R_{\text{in},X}
=
\frac{1}{g_{ds2}-g_{m1}g_{m2}/G_D}
}
\]

so it becomes negative when

\[
\boxed{
g_{m1}g_{m2}>G_Dg_{ds2}.
}
\]

If \(r_{o1},r_{o2}\to\infty\), then approximately

\[
R_{\text{in},X}\simeq
-\frac{1}{g_{m1}g_{m2}R_D}.
\]

This is the usual negative-resistance result for this topology.

---

## Example: high-output branch

Using the long-channel square-law model,

\[
I_D=\beta\left[(V_{GS}-V_T)V_{DS}-\frac{V_{DS}^2}{2}\right]
\]

in triode and

\[
I_D=\frac{\beta}{2}(V_{GS}-V_T)^2
\]

in saturation.

Initially \(M_1\) is off, so \(v_o\simeq V_{DD}\). Normally \(M_2\) is then in triode, giving

\[
I_{\text{in}}
=
\beta_2
\left[
(V_{DD}-V_{T2})v_x-\frac{v_x^2}{2}
\right].
\]

\(M_1\) begins to conduct when \(v_x=V_{T1}\), corresponding approximately to

\[
I_{\text{in,on}}
=
\beta_2
\left[
(V_{DD}-V_{T2})V_{T1}
-\frac{V_{T1}^2}{2}
\right].
\]

That is only the onset of \(M_1\) conduction; the actual regenerative transition generally occurs later, when

\[
G_Dg_{ds2}=g_{m1}g_{m2}.
\]

For the common region in which \(M_1\) is saturated and \(M_2\) is triode,

\[
v_o=V_{DD}
-\frac{R_D\beta_1}{2}(v_x-V_{T1})^2
\]

and the switching point satisfies

\[
V_{DD}-V_{T2}-v_x
=
\frac{R_D\beta_1}{2}
(v_x-V_{T1})(3v_x-V_{T1}).
\]

Substituting that \(v_x\) into the current expression gives the rising-current trip value.

---

## Important practical point

A DC state with \(M_2\) completely off cannot support a nonzero ideal \(I_{\text{in}}\), because node \(X\) then has no DC path:

\[
I_{\text{in}}=I_{D2}
\]

would not be satisfiable.

Consequently, after regeneration drives \(M_2\) off, the eventual low-output state is determined by nonshown effects:

- current-source compliance,
- capacitance at node \(X\),
- leakage/subthreshold current,
- a reset or bleed path,
- finite output resistance of the input source.

So the shown circuit is a regenerative/negative-resistance cell, but a complete static Schmitt trigger or latch requires the input-source model and usually a reset/discharge path at \(X\).

Assuming \(M_1\) and \(M_2\) are NMOS devices with their sources grounded, the important connections are

\[
\begin{array}{c|cc}
 & V_{GS} & V_{DS}\\ \hline
M_1 & V_X & V_{\text{out}}\\
M_2 & V_{\text{out}} & V_X
\end{array}
\]

Thus, \(M_1\) is a resistively loaded common-source stage, and \(M_2\) feeds its output back to node \(X\). The circuit is a cross-coupled, positive-feedback structure.

## DC equations

Because MOS gates draw essentially zero DC current,

\[
I_{\text{in}}=I_{D2}
\]

at node \(X\), and at the output node,

\[
\frac{V_{DD}-V_{\text{out}}}{R_{D1}}=I_{D1}.
\]

Hence the general DC equations are

\[
I_{\text{in}}
=
I_{D2}\left(V_{GS2}=V_{\text{out}},\,V_{DS2}=V_X\right)
\]

and

\[
\frac{V_{DD}-V_{\text{out}}}{R_{D1}}
=
I_{D1}\left(V_{GS1}=V_X,\,V_{DS1}=V_{\text{out}}\right).
\]

These equations must be solved using the proper MOSFET region equations.

---

## Both transistors in saturation

With

\[
I_D=\frac{\beta}{2}(V_{GS}-V_T)^2,
\]

and neglecting channel-length modulation,

\[
I_{\text{in}}
=
\frac{\beta_2}{2}(V_{\text{out}}-V_{T2})^2,
\]

so that

\[
\boxed{
V_{\text{out}}
=
V_{T2}+\sqrt{\frac{2I_{\text{in}}}{\beta_2}}
}
\]

and

\[
\frac{V_{DD}-V_{\text{out}}}{R_{D1}}
=
\frac{\beta_1}{2}(V_X-V_{T1})^2.
\]

Therefore,

\[
\boxed{
V_X
=
V_{T1}
+
\sqrt{
\frac{2(V_{DD}-V_{\text{out}})}
{\beta_1R_{D1}}
}
}
\]

provided that the saturation conditions hold:

\[
V_{\text{out}}\ge V_X-V_{T1},
\qquad
V_X\ge V_{\text{out}}-V_{T2}.
\]

If either condition fails, the corresponding transistor must be analyzed in triode region.

---

## Small-signal analysis

Let

\[
G_1=\frac{1}{R_{D1}}+g_{o1}.
\]

For small signals, \(V_{DD}\) is AC ground. At the output,

\[
G_1v_{\text{out}}+g_{m1}v_x=0,
\]

thus

\[
\boxed{
\frac{v_{\text{out}}}{v_x}
=
-\frac{g_{m1}}{G_1}
}
\]

which is the gain of \(M_1\).

At node \(X\),

\[
i_{\text{in}}=g_{o2}v_x+g_{m2}v_{\text{out}}.
\]

Substitution gives

\[
i_{\text{in}}
=
\left(
g_{o2}
-
\frac{g_{m1}g_{m2}}{G_1}
\right)v_x.
\]

Therefore, the incremental resistance seen by the input current source is

\[
\boxed{
R_{\text{in}}
=
\frac{v_x}{i_{\text{in}}}
=
\frac{1}
{
g_{o2}
-\dfrac{g_{m1}g_{m2}}{1/R_{D1}+g_{o1}}
}
}
\]

and the current-to-output-voltage gain is

\[
\boxed{
\frac{v_{\text{out}}}{i_{\text{in}}}
=
\frac{g_{m1}}
{
g_{m1}g_{m2}
-
(1/R_{D1}+g_{o1})g_{o2}
}
}.
\]

If \(r_{o1},r_{o2}\to\infty\),

\[
\boxed{
R_{\text{in}}\simeq-\frac{1}{g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}}
}
\]

and

\[
\boxed{
\frac{v_{\text{out}}}{i_{\text{in}}}\simeq\frac{1}{g_{m2}}.
}
\]

---

## Positive feedback and stability

A rise in \(V_X\):

1. increases the current of \(M_1\),
2. lowers \(V_{\text{out}}\),
3. decreases the current of \(M_2\),
4. leaves more of \(I_{\text{in}}\) available to charge node \(X\),
5. raises \(V_X\) further.

Thus the loop is regenerative, i.e. positive feedback.

The approximate loop-gain magnitude is

\[
\boxed{
T \simeq
g_{m1}(R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1})\,g_{m2}r_{o2}.
}
\]

The circuit exhibits negative incremental resistance and tends toward regeneration when

\[
\boxed{
g_{m1}g_{m2}
>
\left(\frac{1}{R_{D1}}+g_{o1}\right)g_{o2}.
}
\]

With ideal saturated MOSFETs, \(g_{o2}\) is very small, so this condition is often easily met. In that case, the DC solution obtained from the saturation equations can be an unstable equilibrium; parasitic capacitances, transistor triode operation, current-source compliance, and device nonlinearities determine the final state.

So this circuit is best viewed as a cross-coupled positive-feedback/negative-resistance cell rather than an ordinary linear amplifier.

Assuming \(M_1\) and \(M_2\) are nMOS devices as drawn:

- Their gates are tied together at node \(X\).
- Their drains are tied together at \(V_{\text{out}}\).
- Their sources are grounded.
- Thus, electrically, they are two parallel common-source nMOS transistors loaded by \(R_{D1}\).

Let \(v_x=V_X\) and \(v_o=V_{\text{out}}\). The output-node equation is

\[
\frac{V_{DD}-v_o}{R_{D1}}=I_{D1}(v_x,v_o)+I_{D2}(v_x,v_o).
\]

So, for a specified gate voltage \(v_x\), increasing \(v_x\) increases the pull-down current and lowers \(v_o\).

For matched devices with

\[
\beta_\Sigma=\beta_1+\beta_2,
\]

and neglecting channel-length modulation, if both devices are in saturation,

\[
I_D=\frac{1}{2}\beta_\Sigma(v_x-V_T)^2,
\]

hence

\[
\boxed{
v_o=V_{DD}-\frac{R_{D1}\beta_\Sigma}{2}(v_x-V_T)^2
}
\]

valid while

\[
v_o\ge v_x-V_T.
\]

If the devices enter triode operation, then

\[
\frac{V_{DD}-v_o}{R_{D1}}
=
\beta_\Sigma\left[(v_x-V_T)v_o-\frac{v_o^2}{2}\right].
\]

For identical transistors, the pair is equivalent to one transistor having twice the effective \(W/L\).

---

## Crucial issue: no DC operating point for nonzero \(I_{\rm in}\)

At node \(X\),

\[
I_{\rm in}=I_{G1}+I_{G2}.
\]

For ideal MOSFETs,

\[
I_{G1}=I_{G2}=0.
\]

Therefore, at DC,

\[
\boxed{I_{\rm in}=0}
\]

is required for a static operating point. A nonzero DC current injected into \(X\) has no resistive DC path to ground. It charges the MOS gate capacitances instead.

Thus, as drawn:

- There is no well-defined DC relation \(V_{\text{out}}(I_{\rm in})\).
- For constant positive \(I_{\rm in}\), \(v_x\) rises with time until leakage, an ESD clamp, gate-oxide breakdown, or the current source compliance limit becomes relevant.
- The output starts near \(V_{DD}\) if the transistors are initially off, then falls as \(v_x\) rises above threshold.

With gate capacitances included, approximately,

\[
I_{\rm in}\simeq C_{\rm eff}\frac{dv_x}{dt},
\]

where, including Miller effect,

\[
C_{\rm eff}\approx
C_{gs1}+C_{gs2}+C_{gb1}+C_{gb2}
+(C_{gd1}+C_{gd2})(1-A_v).
\]

Hence,

\[
v_x(t)\approx v_x(0)+\frac{I_{\rm in}}{C_{\rm eff}}t,
\]

and \(v_o(t)\) follows the nonlinear common-source transfer characteristic above.

For a small-signal voltage applied at \(X\), the voltage gain is approximately

\[
\boxed{
\frac{v_o}{v_x}
=
-\frac{g_{m1}+g_{m2}}
{1/R_{D1}+g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}}
}
\]

or, if \(r_o\) is large,

\[
\frac{v_o}{v_x}\approx -(g_{m1}+g_{m2})R_{D1}.
\]

So the circuit is a parallel-nMOS common-source stage, but the current source at \(X\) does not establish a DC bias unless a leakage/bias path from \(X\) is added.

The key feature is that **the circuit has positive feedback**. Both MOSFETs are NMOS devices with grounded sources; \(M_1\) is a common-source stage, and \(M_2\) feeds the output voltage back to node \(X\).

Assume no output load, negligible gate currents, and initially that both transistors operate in saturation.

## 1. Feedback polarity

Consider a small increase in \(V_{\text{out}}\):
\[
V_{\text{out}}\uparrow
\;\Rightarrow\; I_{D2}\uparrow
\;\Rightarrow\; V_X\downarrow
\;\Rightarrow\; I_{D1}\downarrow
\;\Rightarrow\; V_{\text{out}}\uparrow.
\]

The original change is reinforced, so this is **regenerative feedback**, not a conventional negative-feedback transimpedance amplifier.

## 2. DC operating point

Since neither gate draws current,
\[
I_{D2}=I_{\text{in}},\qquad
I_{D1}=\frac{V_{DD}-V_{\text{out}}}{R_{D1}}.
\]

Using the long-channel saturation model
\[
I_D=\frac{\beta}{2}(V_{GS}-V_T)^2,
\]
and neglecting channel-length modulation gives
\[
\boxed{V_{\text{out}}
=V_{T2}+\sqrt{\frac{2I_{\text{in}}}{\beta_2}}}
\]
and
\[
\boxed{V_X
=V_{T1}+
\sqrt{\frac{2(V_{DD}-V_{\text{out}})}
{\beta_1R_{D1}}}}.
\]

These equations describe a **candidate equilibrium**. They require
\[
V_{\text{out}}\ge V_X-V_{T1},
\qquad
V_X\ge V_{\text{out}}-V_{T2},
\qquad
V_{\text{out}}<V_{DD},
\]
and do not establish that the equilibrium is stable.

## 3. Small-signal gain and impedances

Include the transistor output resistances and define
\[
R_1=R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1}.
\]

The two node equations are
\[
i_{\text{in}}=\frac{v_x}{r_{o2}}+g_{m2}v_{\text{out}},
\qquad
v_{\text{out}}=-g_{m1}R_1v_x.
\]

Define the positive loop-gain magnitude
\[
L=g_{m1}g_{m2}R_1r_{o2}.
\]

Then the input resistance and transimpedance are
\[
\boxed{R_{\text{in}}=\frac{v_x}{i_{\text{in}}}
=\frac{r_{o2}}{1-L}}
\]
and
\[
\boxed{Z_t=\frac{v_{\text{out}}}{i_{\text{in}}}
=-\frac{g_{m1}R_1r_{o2}}{1-L}}.
\]

With the input small-signal current set to zero, the output resistance is
\[
\boxed{R_{\text{out}}=\frac{R_1}{1-L}}.
\]

If output resistances are neglected—or, more generally, \(L\gg1\)—the formal low-frequency results become
\[
\boxed{Z_t\approx \frac{1}{g_{m2}}},
\qquad
\boxed{R_{\text{in}}\approx
-\frac{1}{g_{m1}g_{m2}R_1}}.
\]

The negative input resistance is an important sign of the regenerative behavior.

## 4. Stability

With lumped capacitances \(C_X\) and \(C_o\) at the two nodes, the characteristic equation is
\[
\left(sC_X+\frac1{r_{o2}}\right)
\left(sC_o+\frac1{R_1}\right)-g_{m1}g_{m2}=0.
\]

Its constant term is proportional to \(1-L\). Consequently:

- **\(L<1\):** stable in this two-node model.
- **\(L=1\):** regeneration threshold.
- **\(L>1\):** one right-half-plane pole; the equilibrium is unstable.

Thus, the saturated operating point is generally unstable when the loop gain is large. Although static algebra then gives \(Z_t\approx1/g_{m2}\), that result should **not** be interpreted as the gain of a stable linear amplifier. In practice, the circuit moves toward a different operating region or a current-source compliance limit.

The important feature is that **\(M_1\) and \(M_2\) form a positive-feedback loop**, not an ordinary negative-feedback transimpedance amplifier. With no component values specified, the analysis is symbolic.

## 1. Circuit connections and DC bias

Both devices are NMOS transistors with grounded sources:

- \(M_1\): gate at \(X\), drain at \(V_{\text{out}}\).
- \(M_2\): gate at \(V_{\text{out}}\), drain at \(X\).

Neglecting MOS gate currents, Kirchhoff’s current law gives
\[
\boxed{I_{D2}=I_{\text{in}}},\qquad
\boxed{I_{D1}=\frac{V_{DD}-V_{\text{out}}}{R_{D1}}}.
\]

Assume initially that both transistors are in saturation and neglect channel-length modulation. Using
\[
I_D=\frac{\beta}{2}(V_{GS}-V_T)^2,
\qquad \beta=\mu_nC_{\text{ox}}\frac WL,
\]
we obtain
\[
\boxed{V_{\text{out}}
=V_{T2}+\sqrt{\frac{2I_{\text{in}}}{\beta_2}}}
\]
and
\[
\boxed{V_X
=V_{T1}+
\sqrt{\frac{2(V_{DD}-V_{\text{out}})}
{\beta_1R_{D1}}}}.
\]

These are **candidate operating-point equations**. They apply only if the resulting voltages satisfy
\[
V_{\text{out}}\ge V_X-V_{T1}
\quad(M_1\text{ saturated}),
\]
\[
V_X\ge V_{\text{out}}-V_{T2}
\quad(M_2\text{ saturated}),
\]
with both devices on and \(V_{\text{out}}\le V_{DD}\). If not, the appropriate cutoff or triode-region equations must be used.

## 2. Small-signal gain and resistances

Include transistor output resistances and define
\[
R_O=R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1}.
\]

At low frequencies, with no external output load,
\[
v_{\text{out}}=-g_{m1}R_Ov_x,
\]
while KCL at \(X\) gives
\[
i_{\text{in}}=\frac{v_x}{r_{o2}}+g_{m2}v_{\text{out}}.
\]

Define the positive loop-gain magnitude
\[
L=g_{m1}g_{m2}R_Or_{o2}.
\]

Combining the equations yields the transimpedance
\[
\boxed{
\frac{v_{\text{out}}}{i_{\text{in}}}
=
-\frac{g_{m1}R_Or_{o2}}{1-L}
}.
\]

The input resistance is
\[
\boxed{
R_{\text{in}}=\frac{v_x}{i_{\text{in}}}
=\frac{r_{o2}}{1-L}
}.
\]

The output resistance, with the input current held fixed, is
\[
\boxed{
R_{\text{out}}=\frac{R_O}{1-L}
}.
\]

In the formal high-loop-gain limit,
\[
\frac{v_{\text{out}}}{i_{\text{in}}}\approx\frac{1}{g_{m2}},
\qquad
R_{\text{in}}\approx-\frac{1}{g_{m1}g_{m2}R_O}.
\]
The negative input resistance is a warning that stability must be checked.

## 3. Feedback polarity and stability

Consider a small increase in \(V_X\):
\[
V_X\uparrow
\;\Rightarrow\;
I_{D1}\uparrow
\;\Rightarrow\;
V_{\text{out}}\downarrow
\;\Rightarrow\;
I_{D2}\downarrow.
\]

With \(I_{\text{in}}\) fixed, less current through \(M_2\) means more current charges node \(X\), driving \(V_X\) still higher. Thus the feedback is **regenerative**.

For example, including lumped capacitances \(C_X\) and \(C_O\) at the two nodes gives the characteristic equation
\[
\left(sC_X+\frac1{r_{o2}}\right)
\left(sC_O+\frac1{R_O}\right)
-g_{m1}g_{m2}=0.
\]

Its constant term is
\[
\frac{1-L}{r_{o2}R_O}.
\]
Consequently, in this two-node model:

- **\(L<1\):** the operating point is locally stable.
- **\(L=1\):** a pole lies at zero.
- **\(L>1\):** one pole is in the right half-plane, so the operating point is unstable.

In particular, neglecting \(M_2\)’s output conductance makes the both-on operating point unstable.

**Conclusion:** Although the ideal DC equations suggest a positive current-to-voltage slope of approximately \(1/g_{m2}\), that does not establish a stable amplifier. The circuit has positive feedback; for \(L>1\), disturbances grow until a transistor changes operating region or some circuit limit is reached.

Assume \(M_1\) and \(M_2\) are nMOS devices, with \(M_2\)’s drain at \(X\), gate at \(V_{\text{out}}\), and source at ground. Let the node voltages be \(v_x\) and \(v_o\).

### DC operating point

Neglecting MOS gate current, the input current must be sunk by \(M_2\), while the resistor current is sunk by \(M_1\):
\[
I_{\text{in}}=I_{D2}(v_x,v_o),
\qquad
\frac{V_{DD}-v_o}{R_{D1}}=I_{D1}(v_x,v_o).
\]
These equations, together with the MOSFET I–V characteristics, determine the bias point; no numerical result is possible without device and component values. For example, if both devices are in saturation and channel-length modulation is neglected,
\[
I_{\text{in}}\simeq \frac{\beta_2}{2}(v_o-V_{T2})^2,
\qquad
\frac{V_{DD}-v_o}{R_{D1}}\simeq \frac{\beta_1}{2}(v_x-V_{T1})^2.
\]

### Small-signal behavior

At the bias point, let \(g_{mi}\) and \(g_{oi}=1/r_{oi}\) be the transconductance and output conductance of \(M_i\), and define
\[
G_o=\frac{1}{R_{D1}}+g_{o1}.
\]
With \(V_{DD}\) treated as AC ground, the small-signal node equations are
\[
G_o v_o+g_{m1}v_x=0,
\qquad
i_{\text{in}}=g_{o2}v_x+g_{m2}v_o.
\]
Thus the voltage gain of the \(M_1\) stage is \(v_o/v_x=-A_1\), where \(A_1=g_{m1}/G_o\), and
\[
\frac{v_x}{i_{\text{in}}}
=\frac{1}{g_{o2}-g_{m2}A_1},
\qquad
\frac{v_o}{i_{\text{in}}}
=-\frac{A_1}{g_{o2}-g_{m2}A_1}.
\]

### Feedback and stability

The loop is **positive feedback**: a rise in \(v_x\) makes \(M_1\) pull \(v_o\) down; the lower \(v_o\) weakens \(M_2\), so \(v_x\) rises further for the same input current. The loop factor in this small-signal model is
\[
\mathcal L=\frac{g_{m1}g_{m2}}{G_o g_{o2}}.
\]
If \(\mathcal L\) approaches 1, the incremental gains become very large. For \(\mathcal L>1\), the input resistance is negative and the bias point is regenerative; with ordinary node capacitances, this generally gives an unstable operating point. For example, a two-node RC model has characteristic equation
\[
(sC_x+g_{o2})(sC_o+G_o)-g_{m1}g_{m2}=0,
\]
which is stable only if \(g_{o2}G_o>g_{m1}g_{m2}\).

So this is not automatically a well-behaved linear transimpedance amplifier: its behavior depends strongly on the bias point, device output conductances, and loading.

I_\text{in} = \frac12 \mu_n C_\text{ox} \left(\frac{W}{L}\right)_2 (V_\text{out}-V_{TH})^2.

\]

- \(M_1\): \(V_\text{out} \ge V_X-V_{TH}\)

The loop consists of two inversions:
- \(V_X\uparrow\;\Rightarrow\;I_{D1}\uparrow\;\Rightarrow\;V_\text{out}\downarrow\) (CS stage),
- \(V_\text{out}\downarrow\;\Rightarrow\;I_{D2}\downarrow\;\Rightarrow\;V_X\uparrow\) (current imbalance at node \(X\)).

The **feedback is therefore positive**.  

Including channel-length modulation, the small-signal resistance seen at node \(X\) is
\[
r_X = \frac{1}{g_{ds2}-g_{m2}(g_{m1}R_{D1}')},
\]
where \(R_{D1}'=R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1}\). Whenever the loop gain \(g_{m1}R_{D1}'>g_{ds2}/g_{m2}\) (normally true), \(r_X<0\). The associated closed-loop pole lies in the right half-plane, confirming that the bias point derived above is **unstable (metastable)**.

**Large-Signal Behavior – Bistable Latch**

Because of the regenerative feedback the circuit behaves as a current-triggered latch with two stable states:

1. **Reset state** (\(V_\text{out}\approx V_{DD}\))  
   - \(M_1\) is off (\(V_X<V_{TH}\)).  
   - \(M_2\) operates in the deep-triode region and sinks \(I_\text{in}\).

The square-law expression for \(V_\text{out}\) locates only the metastable point; the circuit does not operate stably there. \[

because the loop gain

\[

\[

\]

That unstable point, for reference only, would be (square law, \(I_D=\tfrac{\beta}{2}(V_{GS}-V_t)^2\), \(\beta=\mu_n C_{ox}W/L\))

\[
V_{out}=V_t+\sqrt{\frac{2I_{in}}{\beta_2}},\qquad V_X=V_t+\sqrt{\frac{2I_{D1}}{\beta_1}},
\]

\[
I_{in}\le I_{\text{crit,H}}=\beta_2\!\left[(V_{DD}-V_t)V_t-\frac{V_t^2}{2}\right].
\]

  It is stable because \(M_1\) is off (\(g_{m1}=0\)), so the loop gain is zero.

- **Low state** (\(M_1\) on, triode): \(M_1\) pulls \(V_{out}\) down and \(M_2\), gated by that low \(V_{out}\), still carries \(I_{in}\). \(M_1\) in triode keeps the loop gain below 1, so this state is stable. It exists only above a lower critical current \(I_{\text{crit,L}}\).

For \(I_{\text{crit,L}}<I_{in}<I_{\text{crit,H}}\) both states exist, so the \(V_{out}\) vs. \(I_{in}\) characteristic has **hysteresis**. Crossing \(I_{\text{crit,H}}\) upward turns \(M_1\) on and the positive feedback snaps the cell to the low state; falling below \(I_{\text{crit,L}}\) snaps it back to the high state.

The schematic is a two-transistor loop, and it is regenerative, not a linear amplifier.

## Connections

- Both devices are grounded-source NMOS (sources at ground, body-effect absent).
- \(I_{in}\) is injected into node \(X\), which is the gate of \(M_1\) and the drain of \(M_2\). So in DC, \(M_2\) is the only path for \(I_{in}\): \(I_{D2}=I_{in}\).
- \(V_{out}\) is the drain of \(M_1\) (pulled up by \(R_{D1}\) to \(V_{DD}\)) and the gate of \(M_2\).

Each device is therefore a common-source stage, and each drives the other's input: \(X \xrightarrow{M_1} V_{out} \xrightarrow{M_2} X\).

## Feedback polarity

A grounded-source stage inverts, so the loop contains two inversions. That is positive (regenerative) feedback. There is no way to get negative feedback here, because both devices can only sink current from their drain nodes.

## DC equilibrium

Neglecting channel-length modulation and assuming saturation, \(M_2\) sets the output directly from the current forced through it:

\[
V_{out}=V_t+\sqrt{\frac{2I_{in}}{k_{n2}}},\qquad k_{n2}=\mu_n C_{ox}\!\left(\frac{W}{L}\right)_2
\]

\(M_1\) then carries whatever \(R_{D1}\) sets, which fixes the drain voltage of \(M_2\):

\[
I_{D1}=\frac{V_{DD}-V_{out}}{R_{D1}},\qquad V_X=V_t+\sqrt{\frac{2I_{D1}}{k_{n1}}}
\]

Saturation of that point needs \(V_X\ge V_{out}-V_t\) (\(M_2\)) and \(V_{out}\ge V_X-V_t\) (\(M_1\)). This is the only DC solution, since \(I_{in}\) must flow through \(M_2\).

## That equilibrium is unstable

Small-signal conductance matrix for \((v_X, v_{out})\), with \(R_L=R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1}\):

\[
\begin{bmatrix} i_{in}\\ i_{out}\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix} 1/r_{o2} & g_{m2}\\ g_{m1} & 1/R_L \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} v_X\\ v_{out}\end{bmatrix}
\]

\[
\det G=\frac{1}{r_{o2}R_L}-g_{m1}g_{m2}=\frac{1-A_1A_2}{r_{o2}R_L}
\]

where \(A_1=g_{m1}R_L\) and \(A_2=g_{m2}r_{o2}\) are the two stage gains. Since \(A_1A_2\gg1\), \(\det G<0\): the eigenvalues have opposite signs, so one is negative.

With capacitances \(C_X\) at \(X\) and \(C_o\) at the output, the source-free characteristic equation is \(\det(G+sC)=0\), i.e.

\[
s^2C_XC_o+s\!\left(\frac{C_X}{R_L}+\frac{C_o}{r_{o2}}\right)+\det G=0.
\]

The constant term is negative, so the product of the roots is negative: one root is in the right half-plane. The bias point is unstable for any realistic sizing (it stays unstable even as \(r_{o2}\to\infty\)).

Equivalently, both ports show negative resistance. With the output open,

\[
r_{in}=\frac{v_X}{i_{in}}\approx-\frac{1}{g_{m1}g_{m2}(R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1})}<0,
\qquad
R_{out}\approx-\frac{1}{g_{m1}g_{m2}r_{o2}}<0.
\]

## Conclusion

It is a negative-resistance/regenerative cell. The closed-form bias above is a valid DC solution but a repelling one: the circuit will not amplify linearly about it. A positive disturbance at \(X\) turns \(M_1\) on harder, drops \(V_{out}\), which starves \(M_2\), which lets \(I_{in}\) charge \(X\) still higher — runaway. It regenerates until the devices leave saturation and the current source's compliance limits it (\(V_X\) driven high, \(V_{out}\) driven low), i.e. latch/Schmitt behavior rather than linear transimpedance gain.

Thus the two common-source stages are cross-coupled. Assume both are NMOS devices in saturation, with \(\lambda=0\), no body effect, and \(V_{DD}\) at AC ground. Let

\[
\beta_i=\mu_nC_{\rm ox}\left(\frac WL\right)_i,\qquad
I_{Di}=\frac{\beta_i}{2}(V_{GSi}-V_{TN})^2,
\qquad
g_{mi}=\beta_i(V_{GSi}-V_{TN}).
\]

---

## 2. DC operating point

At node \(X\), the MOS gates draw no DC current, so all of \(I_{\text{in}}\) flows through \(M_2\):

\[
I_{\text{in}}=I_{D2}
=\frac{\beta_2}{2}(V_{\text{out}}-V_{TN})^2.
\]

Hence

\[
\boxed{V_{\text{out}}=V_{TN}+
\sqrt{\frac{2I_{\text{in}}}{\beta_2}}}.
\]

At the output node,

\[
I_{D1}=\frac{V_{DD}-V_{\text{out}}}{R_{D1}}
=\frac{\beta_1}{2}(V_X-V_{TN})^2,
\]

so

\[
\boxed{
V_X=V_{TN}+
\sqrt{\frac{2}{\beta_1R_{D1}}
\left[
V_{DD}-V_{TN}
-\sqrt{\frac{2I_{\text{in}}}{\beta_2}}
\right]}
}.
\]

These results require

\[
V_{\text{out}}\ge V_X-V_{TN}
\quad\text{and}\quad
V_X\ge V_{\text{out}}-V_{TN}
\]

for \(M_1\) and \(M_2\), respectively, to remain saturated. Also \(V_{\text{out}}<V_{DD}\).

---

## 3. Low-frequency small-signal behavior

Use lowercase \(v_x,v_o,i_{\text{in}}\) for incremental quantities.

### Output node

Since \(M_1\) has gate voltage \(v_x\),

\[
i_{d1}=g_{m1}v_x.
\]

The incremental resistor current is \(-v_o/R_{D1}\), hence

\[
g_{m1}v_x=-\frac{v_o}{R_{D1}},
\]

or

\[
\boxed{\frac{v_o}{v_x}=-g_{m1}R_{D1}}.
\]

This is the gain of the inverting common-source stage \(M_1\).

### Input node

The gate of \(M_2\) is the output node, so

\[
i_{d2}=g_{m2}v_o.
\]

KCL at \(X\) gives

\[
\boxed{i_{\text{in}}=g_{m2}v_o}.
\]

Therefore

\[
\boxed{\frac{v_o}{i_{\text{in}}}=\frac{1}{g_{m2}}}.
\]

Combining the two equations,

\[
v_x=-\frac{v_o}{g_{m1}R_{D1}}
=-\frac{i_{\text{in}}}
{g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}}.
\]

Thus the small-signal resistance seen by the input current source is

\[
\boxed{
R_{\text{in}}=\frac{v_x}{i_{\text{in}}}
=-\frac{1}{g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}}
}.
\]

Equivalently, the input conductance is

\[
\boxed{G_{\text{in}}=-g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}}.
\]

So the circuit synthesizes a **negative resistance**. A positive \(v_x\) lowers \(v_o\), which reduces the current sunk by \(M_2\); consequently current is returned to the test source. The energy comes from \(V_{DD}\).

At the DC operating point,

\[
g_{m2}=\sqrt{2\beta_2 I_{\text{in}}},
\qquad
g_{m1}=
\sqrt{\frac{2\beta_1(V_{DD}-V_{\text{out}})}{R_{D1}}}.
\]

The same negative resistance follows by differentiating the large-signal expression for \(V_X(I_{\text{in}})\).

---

## 4. Feedback and stability

There are two inversions around the cross-coupled loop:

\[
X \xrightarrow{M_1} V_{\text{out}}:\quad -g_{m1}R_y,
\]

\[
V_{\text{out}}\xrightarrow{M_2}X:\quad -g_{m2}R_x,
\]

where

\[
R_y=R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1},\qquad
R_x=r_{o2}\quad\text{(or \(r_{o2}\parallel R_{\text{source}}\))}.
\]

The loop gain is therefore positive:

\[
\boxed{L=g_{m1}g_{m2}R_xR_y}.
\]

With finite output resistances,

\[
R_{\text{in}}=\frac{R_x}{1-L},
\qquad
R_{\text{out}}=\frac{R_y}{1-L},
\]

and

\[
\frac{v_o}{i_{\text{in}}}
=\frac{1}{g_{m2}(1-1/L)}.
\]

For \(L\gg1\), these reduce to \(v_o/i_{\text{in}}\approx1/g_{m2}\) and the negative input resistance found above. In the ideal \(\lambda=0\) case, \(r_{o2}\to\infty\), giving formally \(R_{\text{out}}\to0\).

Because the feedback is regenerative, an isolated bias point with \(L>1\) is generally unstable with parasitic node capacitances; the circuit behaves as a latch/negative-resistance element unless an external source impedance, control loop, or resonator stabilizes it. This is precisely why such a circuit can be used to cancel tank losses in an oscillator.

### Main results

\[
\boxed{\frac{v_{\text{out}}}{i_{\text{in}}}=\frac{1}{g_{m2}}}
\]

\[
\boxed{R_{\text{in}}
=-\frac{1}{g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}}}
\]

\[
\boxed{V_{\text{out,DC}}
=V_{TN}+\sqrt{\frac{2I_{\text{in}}}{\beta_2}}}
\]

under saturation and \(\lambda=0\).

- \(M_1:\; G=X,\; D=V_{\text{out}},\; S=0\)
- \(M_2:\; G=V_{\text{out}},\; D=X,\; S=0\)

Thus \(M_1\) and \(M_2\) form two common-source stages in a closed loop. Let \(R_D\equiv R_{D1}\).

---

## 2. DC operation

Since MOS gates draw no dc current,

\[
I_{D2}=I_{\text{in}},
\qquad
I_{D1}=\frac{V_{DD}-V_{\text{out}}}{R_D}.
\]

Assume square-law saturation, common threshold \(V_T\), \(\lambda=0\), and define

\[
\beta_i=\mu_n C_{\rm ox}\left(\frac WL\right)_i .
\]

Then

\[
I_{D1}=\frac{\beta_1}{2}(V_X-V_T)^2,
\qquad
I_{D2}=\frac{\beta_2}{2}(V_{\text{out}}-V_T)^2.
\]

Consequently,

\[
\boxed{
V_{\text{out}}=V_T+\sqrt{\frac{2I_{\text{in}}}{\beta_2}}
}
\]

and

\[
\boxed{
V_X=V_T+
\sqrt{\frac{2(V_{DD}-V_{\text{out}})}
{\beta_1R_D}}
}.
\]

Interestingly, \(V_{\text{out}}\) is independent of \(M_1\) and \(R_D\) under these idealized assumptions; \(M_1\) and \(R_D\) determine \(V_X\) and whether the transistors remain saturated.

The saturation requirements are

\[
V_{\text{out}}\ge V_X-V_T \quad (M_1),
\qquad
V_X\ge V_{\text{out}}-V_T \quad (M_2).
\]

Outside these ranges, triode-region equations must be used and multiple dc solutions can occur.

With channel-length modulation,

\[
I_{\text{in}}=
\frac{\beta_2}{2}(V_{\text{out}}-V_T)^2(1+\lambda_2V_X),
\]

\[
\frac{V_{DD}-V_{\text{out}}}{R_D}=
\frac{\beta_1}{2}(V_X-V_T)^2(1+\lambda_1V_{\text{out}}),
\]

which generally must be solved simultaneously.

---

## 3. Low-frequency small-signal result

For \(\lambda=0\), let \(g_{m1},g_{m2}\) be the bias transconductances. At the output node,

\[
\frac{v_{\text{out}}}{R_D}+g_{m1}v_x=0
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
v_{\text{out}}=-g_{m1}R_Dv_x .
\]

At node \(X\),

\[
i_{\text{in}}=g_{m2}v_{\text{out}}.
\]

Therefore,

\[
\boxed{\frac{v_{\text{out}}}{i_{\text{in}}}=\frac{1}{g_{m2}}}
\]

and

\[
\boxed{
\frac{v_x}{i_{\text{in}}}
=-\frac{1}{g_{m1}g_{m2}R_D}
}.
\]

The first result agrees with the derivative of the large-signal expression:

\[
\frac{dV_{\text{out}}}{dI_{\text{in}}}
=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\beta_2I_{\text{in}}}}
=\frac{1}{g_{m2}}.
\]

The second result is a **negative input resistance** at \(X\).

---

## 4. Feedback polarity and stability

The feedback is regenerative. For example,

\[
v_x\uparrow
\Rightarrow I_{D1}\uparrow
\Rightarrow v_{\text{out}}\downarrow
\Rightarrow I_{D2}\downarrow
\Rightarrow \text{more input current charges }X
\Rightarrow v_x\uparrow .
\]

Each common-source stage contributes an inversion, so the loop has two inversions and hence positive feedback. It is a shunt-mixed, voltage-sampled feedback loop, but with the wrong sign for an ordinary transimpedance amplifier.

Include finite output conductances:

\[
G_o=\frac1{R_D}+g_{o1},\qquad R_o=\frac1{G_o},
\]

\[
G_x=g_{o2}+g_s,\qquad R_x=\frac1{G_x},
\]

where \(g_s\) is any small-signal conductance of the current source. The small-signal equations are

\[
G_ov_{\text{out}}+g_{m1}v_x=0,
\qquad
G_xv_x+g_{m2}v_{\text{out}}=i_{\text{in}}.
\]

The positive loop gain is

\[
\boxed{L=g_{m1}g_{m2}R_oR_x}.
\]

The low-frequency transimpedance and impedances become

\[
\boxed{
\frac{v_{\text{out}}}{i_{\text{in}}}
=-\frac{g_{m1}R_oR_x}{1-L}
},
\]

\[
\boxed{
R_{\text{in}}=\frac{R_x}{1-L},
\qquad
R_{\text{out}}=\frac{R_o}{1-L}
}.
\]

Thus \(L=1\) gives infinite gain/singular operation, while \(L>1\) gives negative small-signal resistances and an unstable nominal operating point.

With node capacitances \(C_x,C_o\), neglecting \(C_{gd}\),

\[
\frac{v_{\text{out}}}{i_{\text{in}}}(s)
=
-\frac{g_{m1}}
{(G_x+sC_x)(G_o+sC_o)-g_{m1}g_{m2}} .
\]

The characteristic polynomial is

\[
C_xC_os^2+(G_xC_o+G_oC_x)s+G_oG_x(1-L).
\]

Hence the linearized equilibrium is stable only if

\[
\boxed{L<1}.
\]

Typically \(g_{o2}\) is small and \(L\gg1\), so the circuit does not behave as a stable linear amplifier. It behaves as a regenerative latch/Schmitt-trigger-like circuit. Its stable states generally involve one transistor being off or in triode; switching thresholds are obtained from the triode-region equations and the condition \(L=1\).

\[

G_1=G_D+g_{o1},\qquad
G_2=g_{o2}.
\]

i_{\text{in}}=G_2v_x+g_{m2}v_o ,

\[

=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\beta_2 I_{\text{in}}}} .
\]

\[
\boxed{
Z_{\text{in},X}
\simeq -\frac{1}{g_{m1}g_{m2}R_D}
}
\]

when \(r_{o1}\to\infty\). Thus an increase in input current raises \(V_{\text{out}}\) but lowers \(V_X\): the circuit presents a negative differential resistance at \(X\).

### Output impedance

With the input current source set to zero (open-circuited),

\[
\boxed{
Z_{\text{out}}
=\frac{R_D\parallel r_{o1}}{1-T}
}
\]

which is also negative for \(T>1\).

---

There are two common-source inversions around the loop:

\[
v_X\uparrow \Rightarrow v_o\downarrow
\Rightarrow I_{D2}\downarrow
\Rightarrow v_X\uparrow .
\]

- \(T=1\): the low-frequency gain diverges; this is the latch/switching threshold.

\[
(C_Xs+G_2)(C_os+G_1)-g_{m1}g_{m2}=0,
\]

whose constant term is \(G_1G_2(1-T)\). Thus \(T>1\) produces a right-half-plane pole. Since \(g_mr_o\) is normally large, \(T\gg1\) is typical; the circuit therefore behaves as a regenerative/bistable latch or negative-resistance element rather than as a stable linear transimpedance amplifier. |---|---|
| **V_DD** | Supply rail |
| **R_D1** | Between V_DD and the output node **V_out** (this is also the drain of M₁) |
| **M₁** | NMOS: drain → V_out, source → GND, gate → node **X** |
| **M₂** | NMOS: drain → node **X**, source → GND, gate → **V_out** |
| **I_in** | Current source from GND into node **X** |
| **V_out** | Output terminal (drain of M₁, gate of M₂) |

Thus M₁ and M₂ form a **cross‑coupled NMOS pair**: the gate of each transistor is driven by the drain of the other.  
M₁ is loaded by R_D1, while M₂ is loaded by the current source I_in.

---

## 1. DC (Bias) Analysis

Let the transistor parameters be  
\(k=\mu_n C_{ox}(W/L)\) and threshold voltage \(V_{TH}\).  
Neglect body effect and, for the first derivation, channel‑length modulation (\(\lambda\approx 0\)).

### KCL equations
* At node **X** (gate currents are zero):
  \[
  I_{D2}=I_{in}
  \]

* At node **V_out**:
  \[
  I_{D1}=\frac{V_{DD}-V_{out}}{R_{D1}}
  \]

### Transistor I–V (saturation assumed)
\[
I_{D1}=\frac{k}{2}\bigl(V_{GS1}-V_{TH}\bigr)^2
      =\frac{k}{2}\bigl(V_X-V_{TH}\bigr)^2
\]

\[
I_{D2}=\frac{k}{2}\bigl(V_{GS2}-V_{TH}\bigr)^2
      =\frac{k}{2}\bigl(V_{out}-V_{TH}\bigr)^2
\]

### Solving for the operating point
From \(I_{D2}=I_{in}\):
\[
\boxed{V_{out}=V_{TH}+\sqrt{\frac{2I_{in}}{k}}}
\qquad (I_{in}>0)
\]

From \(I_{D1}=(V_{DD}-V_{out})/R_{D1}\):
\[
\boxed{V_X=V_{TH}+\sqrt{\frac{2}{kR_{D1}}\bigl(V_{DD}-V_{out}\bigr)}}
\]

### Saturation conditions
M₁ is in saturation if \(V_{DS1}=V_{out}\ge V_{GS1}-V_{TH}=V_X-V_{TH}\).  
M₂ is in saturation if \(V_{DS2}=V_X\ge V_{GS2}-V_{TH}=V_{out}-V_{TH}\).

If either condition fails, replace the corresponding square‑law by the triode formula
\(I_D=k\bigl[(V_{GS}-V_{TH})V_{DS}-\tfrac12V_{DS}^2\bigr]\).

> **Key DC result:** Once \(I_{in}\) is fixed, \(V_{out}\) is determined **only** by M₂ (it acts as a square‑root current‑to‑voltage converter). The value of \(V_X\) is then set by M₁ and the drop across R_D1.

---

## 2. Small‑Signal (AC) Analysis

Linearize around the DC point. Define small‑signal voltages \(v_{out}\) and \(v_x\).

\[
g_{m1}=k\bigl(V_X-V_{TH}\bigr)=\sqrt{2kI_{D1}},\qquad
g_{m2}=k\bigl(V_{out}-V_{TH}\bigr)=\sqrt{2kI_{in}}
\]

Output resistances (if \(\lambda\neq0\)):
\[
r_{o1}=\frac{1}{\lambda I_{D1}},\qquad r_{o2}=\frac{1}{\lambda I_{D2}}=\frac{1}{\lambda I_{in}}
\]

### Nodal equations
**At X:**
\[
i_{in}= \frac{v_x}{r_{o2}}+g_{m2}v_{out}
\;\;\Longrightarrow\;\;
v_x = r_{o2}\bigl(i_{in}-g_{m2}v_{out}\bigr)
\]

**At V_out** (R_D1, r_o1 and the M₁ current source are in parallel to ground):
\[
\frac{v_{out}}{R_{D1}}+\frac{v_{out}}{r_{o1}}+g_{m1}v_x =0
\;\;\Longrightarrow\;\;
v_x = -v_{out}\left(\frac{1}{R_{D1}}+\frac{1}{r_{o1}}\right)\frac{1}{g_{m1}}
\]

### Transimpedance gain \(v_{out}/i_{in}\)
Eliminating \(v_x\):
\[
\boxed{\frac{v_{out}}{i_{in}}=
\frac{1}{g_{m2}-\dfrac{1}{g_{m1}r_{o2}}\left(\dfrac{1}{R_{D1}}+\dfrac{1}{r_{o1}}\right)}}
\]

If \(r_{o1},r_{o2}\to\infty\) (long‑channel devices):
\[
\boxed{\frac{v_{out}}{i_{in}}\approx \frac{1}{g_{m2}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2kI_{in}}}}
\]

### Output resistance \(R_{out}\) (set \(i_{in}=0\), apply test source \(v_t\))
With \(i_{in}=0\) we have \(v_x=-g_{m2}r_{o2}v_t\). Substituting into the KCL at V_out:
\[
R_{out}=\frac{v_t}{i_t}
=\frac{1}{\displaystyle\frac{1}{R_{D1}}+\frac{1}{r_{o1}}-g_{m1}g_{m2}r_{o2}}
\]

> **Important:** The term \(-g_{m1}g_{m2}r_{o2}\) represents **positive feedback** (an increase in \(v_{out}\) lowers \(v_x\), which reduces \(I_{D1}\) and lets \(v_{out}\) rise further).  
> If
> \[
> g_{m1}g_{m2}r_{o2}>\frac{1}{R_{D1}}+\frac{1}{r_{o1}}
> \]
> then **\(R_{out}<0\)**: the circuit exhibits a negative resistance at the output.

### Input resistance at node X
\[
R_{in}=\frac{v_x}{i_{in}}
= \frac{-r_{o2}\left(\dfrac{1}{R_{D1}}+\dfrac{1}{r_{o1}}\right)/g_{m1}}
       {g_{m2}-\left(\dfrac{1}{R_{D1}}+\dfrac{1}{r_{o1}}\right)/(g_{m1}r_{o2})}
\]

---

## 3. Summary of Circuit Behavior

| Feature | Expression / Condition |
|---|---|
| **DC transfer** | \(V_{out}=V_{TH}+\sqrt{2I_{in}/k}\) (square‑root law) |
| **Bias of M₁** | Set by \(V_X\) via \(I_{D1}=(V_{DD}-V_{out})/R_{D1}\) |
| **Small‑signal gain** | Transimpedance \(\approx 1/g_{m2}\) |
| **Feedback** | Positive (cross‑coupled gates) |
| **Output resistance** | Can be **negative** when \(g_{m1}g_{m2}r_{o2}\) dominates |
| **Operating region** | Both in saturation if \(V_X\ge V_{out}-V_{TH}\) and \(V_{out}\ge V_X-V_{TH}\) |

In short, the circuit is a **cross‑coupled NMOS pair** that converts the input current \(I_{in}\) into an output voltage \(V_{out}\) through the square‑law of M₂, while M₁ together with R_D1 sets the bias point at node X. The cross‑coupling creates positive feedback, giving the circuit a potentially **negative output resistance** in the small‑signal domain.

answer.text:
**Circuit Identification**

The circuit consists of:

* Supply $V_{DD}$ and load resistor $R_{D1}$
* Two MOSFETs $M_1$ and $M_2$ (both $n$-channel enhancement mode, with $M_2$ diode‑connected)
* A DC current source $I_{\mathrm{in}}$ feeding node $X$
* Output node $V_{\mathrm{out}}$

Connections:
* $V_{DD}\rightarrow R_{D1}\rightarrow V_{\mathrm{out}}$
* $M_1$: drain at $V_{\mathrm{out}}$, source at ground, gate at $X$
* $M_2$: drain and gate tied together at $X$, source at ground
* $I_{\mathrm{in}}$ injects current into node $X$ (gate currents are zero, so all of $I_{\mathrm{in}}$ flows through $M_2$)

Thus $M_1$ and $M_2$ form a **current mirror** with mirror ratio $(W/L)_1/(W/L)_2$.  
The resistor $R_{D1}$ converts the mirrored current $I_{D1}$ into the output voltage $V_{\mathrm{out}}$.

---

## 1. DC Analysis (Operating Point)

Assume saturation for both devices (channel‑length modulation $\lambda=0$ is ignored for the basic result; it can be added easily).

### Transistor $M_2$ (diode‑connected, $V_{DS2}=V_{GS2}=V_X$)

Because gate current is zero:
$$I_{D2}=I_{\mathrm{in}}=\frac{1}{2}k_n\left(V_X-V_{THN}\right)^2$$
where $k_n=\mu_n C_{ox}(W/L)_2$.

Solving for the gate‑source voltage (and hence for $V_X$):
$$\boxed{V_X = V_{GS2}=V_{THN}+\sqrt{\frac{2I_{\mathrm{in}}}{k_n}}}$$

Since $V_{DS2}=V_{GS2}>V_{GS2}-V_{THN}$, $M_2$ is always in saturation (for $I_{\mathrm{in}}>0$).

### Transistor $M_1$

$V_{GS1}=V_X$ (sources are both ground). Hence
$$I_{D1}=\frac{1}{2}k_1\left(V_X-V_{THN}\right)^2
      =\frac{k_1}{k_2}\,I_{\mathrm{in}}
      =\frac{(W/L)_1}{(W/L)_2}\,I_{\mathrm{in}}$$

The current through $R_{D1}$ is $I_{R}=I_{D1}$, so
$$\frac{V_{DD}-V_{\mathrm{out}}}{R_{D1}} = \frac{(W/L)_1}{(W/L)_2}\,I_{\mathrm{in}}$$

Therefore the **DC transfer characteristic** is linear:
$$\boxed{V_{\mathrm{out}} = V_{DD}-R_{D1}\,\frac{(W/L)_1}{(W/L)_2}\,I_{\mathrm{in}}}$$

### Saturation condition for $M_1$

$M_1$ remains in saturation provided
$$V_{DS1}=V_{\mathrm{out}} \ge V_{GS1}-V_{THN}=V_X-V_{THN}
\;\;\Longrightarrow\;\;
V_{\mathrm{out}} > \sqrt{\frac{2I_{\mathrm{in}}}{k_2}}$$

If $V_{\mathrm{out}}$ falls below this value, $M_1$ enters the triode region and the relation becomes nonlinear.

---

## 2. Small‑Signal (AC) Analysis

Define the small‑signal parameters at the operating point ($Q$):

$$g_{m1}=k_1\left(V_{GS1Q}-V_{THN}\right),\qquad
  g_{m2}=k_2\left(V_{GS2Q}-V_{THN}\right)=\sqrt{2k_2I_{\mathrm{in}}}$$

$$g_{o1}=\frac{1}{r_{o1}}=\lambda_1 I_{D1Q},\qquad
  g_{o2}=\frac{1}{r_{o2}}=\lambda_2 I_{\mathrm{in}}$$

(Body‑effect terms $g_{mb1},g_{mb2}$ can be added in parallel if the bulks are not tied to the sources.)

### Impedance at node $X$

Because $M_2$ is diode‑connected ($v_{gs2}=v_{ds2}=v_x$):
$$Z_X \approx \frac{1}{g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{o2}}\approx\frac{1}{g_{m2}}$$

Hence
$$v_x = \frac{i_{\mathrm{in}}}{g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{o2}}$$

### KCL at $V_{\mathrm{out}}$

The resistor $R_{D1}$ and transistor $M_1$ (source at $v_{\mathrm{out}}$, drain at AC ground, gate at $v_x$) give:
$$\frac{v_{\mathrm{out}}}{R_{D1}} + \frac{v_{\mathrm{out}}}{r_{o1}} + (g_{m1}+g_{mb1})(v_{\mathrm{out}}-v_x)=0$$

Solving for $v_{\mathrm{out}}$:
$$v_{\mathrm{out}}=\frac{g_{m1}}{\displaystyle\frac{1}{R_{D1}}+g_{o1}+g_{m1}+g_{mb1}}\,v_x$$

### Transimpedance gain $\displaystyle R_m=\frac{v_{\mathrm{out}}}{i_{\mathrm{in}}}$

Combining the two results:
$$\boxed{\frac{v_{\mathrm{out}}}{i_{\mathrm{in}}}
= \frac{g_{m1}}
{\bigl(g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{o2}\bigr)
 \left(\frac{1}{R_{D1}}+g_{o1}+g_{m1}+g_{mb1}\right)}}$$

If channel‑length modulation and body effect are negligible ($\lambda\to0$, $\chi\to0$):
$$\boxed{\frac{v_{\mathrm{out}}}{i_{\mathrm{in}}}
\approx \frac{g_{m1}}{g_{m2}}\,\frac{R_{D1}}{1+g_{m1}R_{D1}}}$$

Two useful limits:
* **Low gain** ($g_{m1}R_{D1}\ll 1$): $\displaystyle \frac{v_{\mathrm{out}}}{i_{\mathrm{in}}}\approx \frac{g_{m1}}{g_{m2}}R_{D1}=R_{D1}\sqrt{\frac{(W/L)_1}{(W/L)_2}}$
* **High gain** ($g_{m1}R_{D1}\gg 1$): $\displaystyle \frac{v_{\mathrm{out}}}{i_{\mathrm{in}}}\approx \frac{1}{g_{m2}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2k_2I_{\mathrm{in}}}}$

Thus the circuit behaves as a **current‑to‑voltage converter** (transimpedance amplifier) whose gain is set primarily by the mirror ratio and the load resistor $R_{D1}$, and ultimately limited by $1/g_{m2}$.

---

## 3. Summary of Key Results

| Quantity | Expression |
|----------|------------|
| $V_X$ | $V_{THN}+\sqrt{2I_{\mathrm{in}}/k_2}$ |
| $I_{D1}$ | $\dfrac{(W/L)_1}{(W/L)_2}I_{\mathrm{in}}$ |
| $V_{\mathrm{out}}$ (DC) | $V_{DD}-R_{D1}\dfrac{(W/L)_1}{(W/L)_2}I_{\mathrm{in}}$ |
| Small‑signal gain $v_{\mathrm{out}}/i_{\mathrm{in}}$ | $\approx \dfrac{g_{m1}}{g_{m2}}\dfrac{R_{D1}}{1+g_{m1}R_{D1}}$ |

The circuit is therefore a **linear (for saturation) current‑controlled voltage source** with the mirror transistor $M_2$ setting the bias point $V_X$ and $M_1$ reproducing the current in the resistive load $R_{D1}$.

answer.text:
**Circuit Identification**

Label the nodes:
- **Vout** – drain of M₁, gate of M₂, and the circuit output
- **X** – drain of M₂, gate of M₁, and the input node
- Both M₁ and M₂ are **n‑channel MOSFETs** with their sources grounded
- R_D1 loads the drain of M₁ from V_DD
- I_in is an independent current source feeding node X

The two transistors are **cross‑coupled**:  
Gate(M₁) = V_X,  Drain(M₁) = Vout → Gate(M₂)  
Gate(M₂) = Vout, Drain(M₂) = V_X

Because gate currents are zero, KCL at X gives I_D2 ≈ I_in.

---

## 1. DC Operating Point (Saturation Assumed)

Write the square‑law (with channel‑length modulation λ):

\[
I_{D1}=K_1\bigl(V_X-V_{TH}\bigr)^2\bigl(1+\lambda_1 V_{out}\bigr)
\]

\[
I_{D2}=K_2\bigl(V_{out}-V_{TH}\bigr)^2\bigl(1+\lambda_2 V_X\bigr)
\]

where \(K_i=\tfrac12\mu_n C_{ox}(W/L)_i\).

**KCL equations**

At X: \(I_{in}=I_{D2}\)

At Vout: \(\displaystyle \frac{V_{DD}-V_{out}}{R_{D1}}=I_{D1}\)

Hence

\[
\boxed{V_{out}=V_{TH}+\sqrt{\frac{I_{in}}{K_2\bigl(1+\lambda_2 V_X\bigr)}}}
\]

\[
\boxed{V_X=V_{TH}+\sqrt{\frac{V_{DD}-V_{out}}{R_{D1}K_1\bigl(1+\lambda_1 V_{out}\bigr)}}}
\]

If \(\lambda_1=\lambda_2=0\) (long‑channel approximation):

\[
V_{out}\approx V_{TH}+\sqrt{\frac{I_{in}}{K_2}},\qquad
V_X\approx V_{TH}+\sqrt{\frac{V_{DD}-V_{out}}{R_{D1}K_1}}
\]

**Saturation checks**
\[
V_{DS1}=V_{out}\ge V_{ov1}=V_{GS1}-V_{TH},\qquad
V_{DS2}=V_X\ge V_{ov2}=V_{GS2}-V_{TH}
\]

*Key point:* Ignoring λ, **Vout is set solely by I_in**; R_D1 and M₁ only determine the bias point V_X.

---

## 2. Small‑Signal (AC) Analysis

Use the standard NMOS small‑signal model (\(g_{mi}=2I_{Di}/V_{ovi}\), \(r_{oi}=1/\lambda I_{Di}\), \(g_{oi}=1/r_{oi}\)).

Denote small‑signal voltages \(v_x,v_{out}\) and input current \(i_{in}\).

### Nodal equations

**Node X:**
\[
i_{in}=g_{m2}v_{out}+g_{o2}v_x
\tag{1}
\]

**Node Vout** (R_D1 → AC ground):
\[
\frac{v_{out}}{R_{D1}}+g_{m1}v_x+g_{o1}v_{out}=0
\;\;\Longrightarrow\;\;
v_x=-v_{out}\frac{1/R_{D1}+g_{o1}}{g_{m1}}
\tag{2}
\]

### Transimpedance gain \(R_m=v_{out}/i_{in}\)

Substitute (2) into (1):

\[
i_{in}=v_{out}\!\left[g_{m2}-\frac{g_{o2}}{g_{m1}}\Bigl(\frac1{R_{D1}}+g_{o1}\Bigr)\right]
\]

\[
\boxed{R_m=\frac{v_{out}}{i_{in}}=
\frac{1}{g_{m2}-\dfrac{g_{o2}}{g_{m1}}\Bigl(\dfrac1{R_{D1}}+g_{o1}\Bigr)}}
\]

For long channels (\(g_{o1},g_{o2}\to0\)):

\[
\boxed{R_m\approx\frac{1}{g_{m2}}=\frac{V_{ov2}}{2I_{D2}}}
\]

So the circuit is a **current‑to‑voltage converter** with gain ≈ 1/g_m2.

### Output resistance \(R_{out}\) (set \(i_{in}=0\))

From (1) with \(i_{in}=0\):
\[
v_x=-\frac{g_{m2}}{g_{o2}}\,v_{out}
\]

Apply a test source \(v_t\) at Vout; the current entering is \(i_t\):

\[
i_t=\frac{v_t}{R_{D1}}+g_{m1}v_x+g_{o1}v_t
=v_t\!\left[\frac1{R_{D1}}+g_{o1}-\frac{g_{m1}g_{m2}}{g_{o2}}\right]
\]

\[
\boxed{R_{out}=\frac{v_t}{i_t}=
\frac{1}{\dfrac1{R_{D1}}+g_{o1}-\dfrac{g_{m1}g_{m2}}{g_{o2}}}}
\]

If \(R_{D1}\to\infty\) and \(g_{o1}\to0\):

\[
\boxed{R_{out}\approx -\frac{g_{o2}}{g_{m1}g_{m2}}=-\frac{1}{g_{m1}(g_{m2}r_{o2})}}
\]

The negative sign shows **positive feedback** through \(r_{o2}\).  
If \(\lambda=0\) exactly (\(g_{o2}=0\)), then \(v_{out}=i_{in}/g_{m2}\) is “stiff” and

\[
\boxed{R_{out}=0}
\]

(i.e. an ideal current‑controlled voltage source).

### Input resistance at X

\[
R_{in}=\frac{v_x}{i_{in}}\approx
-\frac{1/R_{D1}+g_{o1}}{g_{m1}g_{m2}}
\;\;\xrightarrow{g_o\to0}\;\;
\boxed{R_{in}\approx -\frac{1}{g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}}}
\]

(very small, negative).

---

## 3. Summary of Behavior

| Quantity | Exact (small‑signal) | Long‑channel (\(\lambda=0\)) |
|----------|----------------------|------------------------------|
| **DC Vout** | \(V_{TH}+\sqrt{I_{in}/[K_2(1+\lambda_2V_X)]}\) | \(V_{TH}+\sqrt{I_{in}/K_2}\) |
| **Transimpedance** \(R_m=v_{out}/i_{in}\) | \(\displaystyle\frac{1}{g_{m2}-\frac{g_{o2}}{g_{m1}}(\frac1{R_{D1}}+g_{o1})}\) | \(1/g_{m2}\) |
| **Output resistance** \(R_{out}\) | \(\displaystyle\Bigl[\frac1{R_{D1}}+g_{o1}-\frac{g_{m1}g_{m2}}{g_{o2}}\Bigr]^{-1}\) | \(0\) |
| **Input resistance** \(R_{in}\) | \(\approx -\frac{1/R_{D1}+g_{o1}}{g_{m1}g_{m2}}\) | \(\approx -1/(g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1})\) |

**Physical interpretation:**  
M₂ acts as a voltage‑controlled current source (transconductance \(g_{m2}\)) that converts the input current into a voltage at Vout. M₁ together with R_D1 forms a bias branch that sets the operating point V_X but, to first order, does not affect the I→V conversion. The cross‑coupling through the finite output resistances \(r_{o1},r_{o2}\) introduces a weak positive feedback, giving a small negative contribution to R_out. Ignoring channel‑length modulation, the circuit behaves as an **ideal transimpedance stage** with gain \(1/g_{m2}\) and zero output impedance.

answer.text:
Looking at the schematic, the circuit consists of:

- **V_DD** and load resistor **R_D1** connected to output node **V_out**.
- **M₁**: NMOS transistor, gate = node **X**, source = GND, drain = **V_out**.
- **M₂**: NMOS transistor, gate = **V_out**, source = GND, drain = node **X**.
- **i_in**: Independent DC (or signal) current source injecting current **into node X** from ground.

Thus **M₁** and **M₂** form a **cross-coupled (positive-feedback) NMOS pair**, biased by **i_in** and loaded by **R_D1**.

---

## 1. DC Operating-Point Analysis

Assume both transistors operate in **saturation** with identical parameters
$$K = \frac{1}{2}\mu_n C_{ox}\left(\frac{W}{L}\right), \qquad V_{th}, \qquad \lambda \approx 0 \ (\text{for simplicity}).$$

### KCL Equations
- **At node X:** The only DC path to ground is through **M₂** (gate draws zero current).
  $$\boxed{I_{D2} = i_{in}}$$
- **At V_out:** Current from R_D1 equals M₁ drain current.
  $$\boxed{I_{D1} = \frac{V_{DD} - V_{out}}{R_{D1}}}$$

### Transistor Currents
- **M₂:** $V_{GS2}=V_{out}$, $V_{DS2}=V_X$
  $$I_{D2} = K(V_{out}-V_{th})^2 \;\Rightarrow\; \boxed{V_{out} = V_{th} + \sqrt{\frac{i_{in}}{K}}} \tag{1}$$
- **M₁:** $V_{GS1}=V_X$, $V_{DS1}=V_{out}$
  $$I_{D1} = K(V_X-V_{th})^2 \;\Rightarrow\; \boxed{V_X = V_{th} + \sqrt{\frac{V_{DD}-V_{out}}{R_{D1}K}}} \tag{2}$$

### Validity Conditions (Saturation)
- **M₂:** $V_{DS2} \ge V_{GS2}-V_{th} \;\Rightarrow\; V_X \ge V_{out}-V_{th}$.
  Using (1)–(2) this requires $I_{D1} \ge i_{in}$.
- **M₁:** $V_{DS1} \ge V_{GS1}-V_{th} \;\Rightarrow\; V_{out} \ge V_X-V_{th}$.

If $i_{in}$ is too large, **M₂ enters triode** and (1) becomes a quadratic involving both $V_{out}$ and $V_X$.

### Key DC Insight
Because **M₂’s gate senses V_out**, its drain current is set directly by $i_{in}$. Thus **V_out is primarily determined by the input current** via (1), while $V_X$ is “slaved” to $I_{D1}$ through (2). The resistor $R_{D1}$ sets $I_{D1}$ but does **not** directly set $V_{out}$ (as long as M₂ stays in saturation).

---

## 2. Small-Signal Analysis

Use small-signal parameters evaluated at the DC bias:
$$g_{m1}, \ g_{m2}, \ r_{o1}=\frac{1}{\lambda I_{D1}}, \ r_{o2}=\frac{1}{\lambda I_{D2}}.$$

The small-signal equivalent has:
- $i_{in}$ as the input signal (current source).
- $R_{D1}$ to AC ground.
- $v_x$ at node X, $v_{out}$ at output.

### KCL (small-signal)
**Node X:**
$$i_{in} = g_{m2}v_{out} + \frac{v_x}{r_{o2}} \tag{3}$$

**Node V_out:**
$$\frac{v_{out}}{R_{D1}} + \frac{v_{out}}{r_{o1}} + g_{m1}v_x = 0 \tag{4}$$

### Transfer Resistance ($v_{out}/i_{in}$)
Solving (3)–(4) for $v_{out}$:

$$\boxed{ \frac{v_{out}}{i_{in}} = \frac{-g_{m1}r_{o2}}{\frac{1}{R_{D1}}+\frac{1}{r_{o1}}-g_{m1}g_{m2}r_{o2}} }$$

**Special case (long channel, $\lambda \to 0$, so $r_o \to \infty$):**
The denominator diverges to $-g_{m1}g_{m2}r_{o2}$, yielding
$$\boxed{ \frac{v_{out}}{i_{in}} \approx \frac{1}{g_{m2}} }$$
This is exactly the derivative of (1): $\frac{dV_{out}}{di_{in}} = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{K i_{in}}} = 1/g_{m2}$.

### Output Resistance ($R_{out}$)
Turn off $i_{in}$ (open it). Applying a test voltage $v_t$ at $V_{out}$:

$$\boxed{ R_{out} = \left[ \frac{1}{R_{D1}}+\frac{1}{r_{o1}} - g_{m1}g_{m2}r_{o2} \right]^{-1} }$$

Because $g_{m1}g_{m2}r_{o2} \gg (1/R_{D1}+1/r_{o1})$ typically, the term in brackets is **negative**, so:

$$\boxed{ R_{out} < 0}$$

The cross-coupled pair acts as a **negative-resistance** element due to **positive feedback**.

---

## 3. Feedback & Stability

The loop is:
$$v_{out} \xrightarrow{g_{m2}} i_{d2} \xrightarrow{r_{o2}} v_x \xrightarrow{g_{m1}} i_{d1} \xrightarrow{R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1}} v_{out}$$

**Loop gain** (breaking the loop at $v_{out}$):
$$L = g_{m1}g_{m2}r_{o2}(R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1})$$

- **If $L < 1$:** The DC solution in saturation is stable; small-signal $R_{out}$ is finite negative but not catastrophic.
- **If $L > 1$:** The positive feedback is too strong. The circuit **latches** into one of two bistable states (e.g., M₁ fully on / M₂ off, or vice versa), and the small-signal resistance becomes unstable.

Thus, **design requires** $g_{m1}g_{m2}r_{o2}R_{D1} < 1$ (approximately) to maintain a unique operating point.

---

## 4. Summary of Function

| Feature | Result |
|---|---|
| **DC $V_{out}$** | $V_{th}+\sqrt{i_{in}/K}$ (set by M₂) |
| **DC $V_X$** | $V_{th}+\sqrt{(V_{DD}-V_{out})/(R_{D1}K)}$ (set by M₁) |
| **Small-signal gain** | $v_{out}/i_{in} \approx 1/g_{m2}$ (transimpedance) |
| **Output resistance** | Negative ($R_{out}<0$) due to cross-coupling |
| **Stability** | Positive feedback loop; need $L<1$ to avoid bistability |

In short, **M₂ acts as a voltage-controlled current source that converts $i_{in}$ to $V_{out}$**, while **M₁ and R_D1 provide the load path**. The cross-coupled architecture is the classic building block of **Schmitt triggers** and **bistable latches**; here it is biased by a current source to establish a controlled, but potentially unstable, DC operating point.

This is a **MOSFET-based transimpedance (current-to-voltage) stage** (or a current-mirror biased common-source amplifier). Based on the topology:

* **$M_1$** is an NMOS common-source transistor: Gate = node **X**, Drain = $V_{out}$, Source = GND.
* **$M_2$** is a **diode-connected** NMOS: Gate & Drain are tied together at node **X**, Source = GND.
* **$i_{in}$** is an independent current source injecting current into node X.
* **$R_{D1}$** is the resistive load from $V_{DD}$ to $V_{out}$.

Because the gate of $M_1$ draws zero DC current, $i_{in}$ must flow entirely through the diode-connected transistor $M_2$ to ground. Thus $M_2$ converts $i_{in}$ into a gate-source voltage $V_X$, which in turn biases $M_1$.

Below is a systematic DC and small-signal analysis.

---

## 1. DC Operating-Point Analysis

Use the long-channel saturation model for both NMOS devices:
$$I_D = \frac{1}{2}k_n(V_{GS}-V_{th})^2, \qquad k_n=\mu_n C_{ox}\left(\frac{W}{L}\right)$$

### Transistor $M_2$ (diode-connected)
Because $V_{DS2}=V_{GS2}=V_X$ and it operates in saturation:
$$i_{in} = \frac{k_{n2}}{2}\left(V_X - V_{th}\right)^2$$
Solving for the node voltage:
$$\boxed{V_X = V_{th} + \sqrt{\frac{2\,i_{in}}{k_{n2}}}}$$

### Transistor $M_1$
Its gate is at $V_X$ and its source is grounded:
$$I_{D1} = \frac{k_{n1}}{2}\left(V_X - V_{th}\right)^2 = \frac{k_{n1}}{k_{n2}}\,i_{in}$$

If the devices are matched ($k_{n1}=k_{n2}$), then **$I_{D1} = i_{in}$** (a 1:1 current mirror).

### Output Voltage
$$V_{out} = V_{DD} - I_{D1}R_{D1}$$
For matched devices:
$$\boxed{V_{out} = V_{DD} - i_{in}R_{D1}}$$

### Saturation Constraints
* **$M_2$:** Automatically in saturation because $V_{DS2}=V_{GS2} \ge V_{GS2}-V_{th}$.
* **$M_1$:** Must satisfy $V_{DS1} \ge V_{GS1}-V_{th}$, i.e.
  $$V_{out} \ge V_X - V_{th} \;\Rightarrow\; V_{DD} - I_{D1}R_{D1} \ge V_X - V_{th}.$$
  This sets the maximum allowable $i_{in}$ before $M_1$ enters triode.

---

## 2. Small-Signal Analysis

Draw the AC equivalent with $V_{DD}$ grounded.

| Element | Small-Signal Model |
|---|---|
| **$M_2$ (diode)** | Between X and GND: resistance $r_{d2} = \frac{1}{g_{m2}}$ (ignoring $r_{o2}$ for simplicity, or $r_{d2}=1/g_{m2}\parallel r_{o2}$) |
| **$M_1$** | Voltage-controlled current source $g_{m1}v_x$, output resistance $r_{o1}$ |
| **$R_{D1}$** | Resistor to ground |

### Node X Equation
The input current $i_{in}$ (small-signal) enters node X and leaves through $M_2$:
$$v_x = i_{in}\left(\frac{1}{g_{m2}} \parallel r_{o2}\right) \approx \frac{i_{in}}{g_{m2}}$$

### Output Node
The common-source transistor pulls current from $V_{out}$:
$$v_{out} = -g_{m1}v_x \left(R_{D1} \parallel r_{o1}\right)$$

Substituting $v_x$:
$$\boxed{v_{out} = -\frac{g_{m1}}{g_{m2}}\left(R_{D1} \parallel r_{o1}\right)i_{in}}$$

For **matched** transistors ($g_{m1}=g_{m2}=g_m$) and $r_{o1} \gg R_{D1}$:
$$\boxed{\frac{v_{out}}{i_{in}} \approx -R_{D1}}$$

The circuit therefore behaves as a **linear transimpedance amplifier** with gain magnitude set by $R_{D1}$.

### Transconductances (evaluated at the DC bias)
$$g_{m1} = \sqrt{2k_{n1}I_{D1}}, \qquad g_{m2} = \sqrt{2k_{n2}i_{in}}$$

---

## 3. Impedances

* **Input impedance** at node X:
  $$R_{in} = \frac{v_x}{i_{in}} = \frac{1}{g_{m2}} \parallel r_{o2} \approx \frac{1}{g_{m2}}$$
  This is typically a few hundred ohms to $\sim$1 kΩ.

* **Output impedance** at $V_{out}$:
  $$R_{out} = R_{D1} \parallel r_{o1}$$

---

## 4. Key Takeaways & Physical Interpretation

| Feature | Description |
|---|---|
| **Function** | Converts an input **current** $i_{in}$ into an output **voltage** $V_{out}$. It is essentially a **current-controlled common-source stage**. |
| **Linearity** | Because $V_X \propto \sqrt{i_{in}}$ while $I_{D1} \propto (V_X-V_{th})^2$, the square-root nonlinearity cancels. For matched devices, $I_{D1}$ is exactly proportional to $i_{in}$, making $V_{out}$ linear with $i_{in}$. |
| **Gain** | Transresistance gain is $-R_{D1}$ (when matched). It is set by a passive resistor, making the gain predictable and independent of transistor parameters (to first order). |
| **Biasing** | $M_2$ acts as a **diode-connected load/reference** that establishes the gate bias for $M_1$ without requiring an external voltage source. |
| **Applications** | Photodiode front-ends, current-output DAC interfaces, and active current-to-voltage converters in analog/mixed-signal design. |

If $k_{n1} \neq k_{n2}$, the DC current relationship is scaled by the $W/L$ ratio:
$$I_{D1} = i_{in}\frac{(W/L)_1}{(W/L)_2}, \qquad v_{out}/i_{in} = -\sqrt{\frac{k_{n1}}{k_{n2}}}\left(R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1}\right)$$

In summary: **$M_2$ diode-converts $i_{in}$ to $V_X$; $M_1$ amplifies $V_X$ as a common-source stage; $R_{D1}$ performs the current-to-voltage conversion at the output.**

This figure is a **MOS current-mirror biased common-source (CS) stage** (or a **transresistance amplifier** driven by a current input). Here is a step-by-step analysis.

---

## 1. Circuit Identification

| Component | Role / Connection |
|-----------|-------------------|
| **$M_1$** | NMOS transistor: **gate** = node $X$, **source** = GND, **drain** = $V_{out}$ |
| **$M_2$** | NMOS transistor: **diode-connected** (gate shorted to drain at node $X$), **source** = GND |
| **$R_{D1}$** | Drain load resistor to $V_{DD}$ |
| **$i_{in}$** | Ideal DC / small-signal current source injecting into node $X$ |
| **$V_{out}$** | Output node (open circuit, no external load shown) |

Because $M_2$ is diode-connected, it provides a DC path to ground for $i_{in}$ and sets a gate-source voltage $V_{GS}$ that is shared by both transistors.

---

## 2. DC Operating-Point Analysis

### Node $X$ (KCL)
MOS gates draw zero DC current, so the entire input current must flow through $M_2$:
$$\boxed{I_{D2} = i_{in}}$$

### $M_2$ (diode-connected NMOS)
Assuming $M_2$ is in **saturation**:
$$I_{D2} = \frac{1}{2}\mu_n C_{ox}\left(\frac{W}{L}\right)_2 (V_{GS} - V_{th})^2$$

Solving for the node voltage:
$$\boxed{V_X = V_{GS} = V_{th} + \sqrt{\frac{2\,i_{in}}{\mu_n C_{ox}(W/L)_2}}}$$

### $M_1$ (common-source NMOS)
Since $V_{GS1} = V_X$ (shared gate node, both sources grounded):
$$I_{D1} = \frac{1}{2}\mu_n C_{ox}\left(\frac{W}{L}\right)_1 (V_{GS} - V_{th})^2 = i_{in}\,\frac{(W/L)_1}{(W/L)_2}$$

If the two devices are **matched** ($W/L$ identical), then:
$$\boxed{I_{D1} = i_{in}}$$

### Output node $V_{out}$ (KCL)
With $V_{out}$ open:
$$\frac{V_{DD} - V_{out}}{R_{D1}} = I_{D1}$$

$$\boxed{V_{out} = V_{DD} - I_{D1}R_{D1} = V_{DD} - i_{in}\,\frac{(W/L)_1}{(W/L)_2}R_{D1}}$$

### Saturation (Active-Region) Conditions
- **$M_2$**: $V_{DS2} = V_X \ge V_{GS}-V_{th}$  → always satisfied.
- **$M_1$**: $V_{DS1} = V_{out} \ge V_{GS}-V_{th}$.

Using the matched case ($I_{D1}=i_{in}$):
$$V_{out} \ge V_{GS} - V_{th} \quad\Rightarrow\quad R_{D1} \le \frac{V_{DD} - (V_{GS}-V_{th})}{i_{in}}$$
If $R_{D1}$ is too large, $M_1$ enters **triode** (linear) region.

---

## 3. Small-Signal Analysis ($i_{in}$ has an AC component $\hat{i}_{in}$)

Replace DC sources with AC ground ($V_{DD} \to$ GND). Use small-signal parameters $g_m$ and $r_o$.

### Equivalent at Node $X$
The diode-connected $M_2$ presents a small-signal resistance:
$$r_{eq2} = \frac{1}{g_{m2} + 1/r_{o2}} \approx \frac{1}{g_{m2}}$$

Because the gate of $M_1$ draws no current:
$$\hat{v}_X = \hat{i}_{in} \cdot r_{eq2} \approx \frac{\hat{i}_{in}}{g_{m2}}$$

### Common-Source Stage $M_1$
$$\hat{v}_{gs1} = \hat{v}_X$$

The controlled drain current is $g_{m1}\hat{v}_{gs1}$. At $V_{out}$ the load is $R_{D1} \parallel r_{o1}$:
$$\hat{v}_{out} = -g_{m1}\hat{v}_{gs1}(R_{D1} \parallel r_{o1})$$

Substituting $\hat{v}_{gs1} = \hat{i}_{in}/g_{m2}$:
$$\boxed{\frac{\hat{v}_{out}}{\hat{i}_{in}} \approx -\frac{g_{m1}}{g_{m2}}\,(R_{D1} \parallel r_{o1})}$$

**If $M_1$ and $M_2$ are matched and biased at the same $I_D = i_{in}$** ($g_{m1}=g_{m2}$):
$$\boxed{\frac{\hat{v}_{out}}{\hat{i}_{in}} \approx -R_{D1}} \quad (\text{assuming } r_{o1} \gg R_{D1})$$

Thus the circuit acts as a **transresistance amplifier** with gain magnitude $\approx R_{D1}$.

### Key Small-Signal Metrics
| Parameter | Expression |
|-----------|------------|
| Input resistance at $X$ | $R_{in} \approx 1/g_{m2}$ |
| Output resistance | $R_{out} = R_{D1} \parallel r_{o1}$ |
| Voltage gain (if $v_{in}$ applied at $X$) | $A_v = -g_{m1}R_{out}$ |
| **Transresistance gain** $v_{out}/i_{in}$ | $\approx -R_{D1}$ (matched) |

---

## 4. Physical Interpretation / Function

- **Bias function:** $M_2$ converts the reference current $i_{in}$ into a $V_{GS}$ voltage. $M_1$ replicates (or scales) that current.
- **Amplification:** Because $M_1$ is a common-source stage with resistive load $R_{D1}$, a small change $\hat{i}_{in}$ changes $V_{GS}$, which modulates $I_{D1}$, producing a voltage swing $\hat{v}_{out} \approx -\hat{i}_{in}R_{D1}$ at the output.
- **Result:** The circuit is a **current-controlled voltage source** (transimpedance stage). If $M_1$ and $M_2$ are identical, the small-signal transfer is simply $\hat{v}_{out}/\hat{i}_{in} \approx -R_{D1}$.

---

### Quick Design Check (Example Numbers)
Suppose $i_{in} = 100\,\mu\text{A}$, $V_{th}=0.5\,$V, $\mu_n C_{ox}(W/L)=200\,\mu\text{A/V}^2$:
- $V_{GS} = 0.5 + \sqrt{2(100)/200} = 1.5\,$V
- With $R_{D1}=5\,$k$\Omega$ and $V_{DD}=3.3\,$V:
  - $V_{out} = 3.3 - 0.1\text{mA}\times 5\text{k}\Omega = 2.8\,$V
  - $V_{DS1}=2.8\,$V $\ge V_{GS}-V_{th}=1.0\,$V → **saturation satisfied**.
  - $g_m \approx 2I_D/(V_{GS}-V_{th}) = 0.2\,$mA/$1\,$V $= 0.2\,$mS.
  - Small-signal gain $\approx -5\,$k$\Omega$.

Assume low-frequency operation, negligible body effect, and no external load at \(V_{\text{out}}\). The important bias connections are

\[
V_{GS1}=V_X,\qquad V_{GS2}=V_{\text{out}},\qquad V_{DS2}=V_X .
\]

\(M_1\) is a common-source stage with drain load \(R_{D1}\); \(M_2\) senses \(V_{\text{out}}\) and returns an output-dependent current to node \(X\).

## 1. DC operating point

Because MOS gates draw no DC current,

\[
I_{D2}=I_{\text{in}},\qquad
I_{D1}=\frac{V_{DD}-V_{\text{out}}}{R_{D1}}.
\]

If both devices are saturated and channel-length modulation is neglected, define \(k_i=\mu_nC_{\text{ox}}(W/L)_i\). Then

\[
I_{\text{in}}=\frac{k_2}{2}(V_{\text{out}}-V_{TH2})^2,
\]

so

\[
\boxed{V_{\text{out}}\approx V_{TH2}+
\sqrt{\frac{2I_{\text{in}}}{k_2}}}
\]

and

\[
\frac{V_{DD}-V_{\text{out}}}{R_{D1}}
=\frac{k_1}{2}(V_X-V_{TH1})^2,
\]

giving

\[
\boxed{V_X\approx V_{TH1}+
\sqrt{\frac{2(V_{DD}-V_{\text{out}})}{k_1R_{D1}}}} .
\]

The saturation conditions are

\[
V_{\text{out}}\ge V_X-V_{TH1}\quad(M_1),
\qquad
V_X\ge V_{\text{out}}-V_{TH2}\quad(M_2).
\]

## 2. Low-frequency small-signal analysis

Let

\[
R_p=R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1}.
\]

KCL at the output gives

\[
\frac{v_o}{R_{D1}}+\frac{v_o}{r_{o1}}+g_{m1}v_X=0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
v_o=-g_{m1}R_p\,v_X .
\]

At node \(X\), the small-signal drain current of \(M_2\) is \(g_{m2}v_o+v_X/r_{o2}\). Hence

\[
i_{\text{in}}=g_{m2}v_o+\frac{v_X}{r_{o2}}.
\]

Eliminating \(v_X\), the transimpedance is

\[
\boxed{
Z_t\equiv\frac{v_o}{i_{\text{in}}}
=\frac{1}{g_{m2}-\dfrac{1}{g_{m1}R_pr_{o2}}}
=\frac{-g_{m1}R_pr_{o2}}{1-T}
}
\]

where

\[
\boxed{T=g_{m1}g_{m2}R_pr_{o2}} .
\]

The corresponding input and output resistances are

\[
\boxed{R_{\text{in}}=\frac{v_X}{i_{\text{in}}}
=\frac{r_{o2}}{1-T}}
\]

and, with the input current source set to zero (open-circuited),

\[
\boxed{R_{\text{out}}=\frac{R_p}{1-T}} .
\]

With feedback removed (\(g_{m2}=0\)), these reduce to \(R_{\text{in}}=r_{o2}\), \(R_{\text{out}}=R_p\), and \(Z_t=-g_{m1}R_pr_{o2}\), as expected.

### Often-used idealized result

If channel-length modulation of \(M_2\) is neglected, \(r_{o2}\rightarrow\infty\), and therefore

\[
\boxed{\frac{v_o}{i_{\text{in}}}\approx\frac{1}{g_{m2}}},
\qquad
\boxed{\frac{v_X}{i_{\text{in}}}\approx
-\frac{1}{g_{m1}g_{m2}R_p}} .
\]

## 3. Feedback polarity and stability

Topologically, \(M_2\) provides **shunt–shunt feedback**: its gate senses the output voltage, and its drain returns a current to the input node.

For the circuit exactly as drawn, however, the feedback is **positive (regenerative)**:

1. \(v_X\uparrow\) increases \(I_{D1}\), so \(v_o\downarrow\).
2. Lower \(v_o\) reduces \(I_{D2}\).
3. With \(i_{\text{in}}\) fixed, less current is drawn from \(X\), tending to raise \(v_X\) further.

Thus the loop transmission is \(+T\), explaining the \(1-T\) denominators. For \(T<1\), the circuit can remain below the regenerative threshold. At \(T=1\), the ideal low-frequency gain diverges; for \(T>1\), the nominal saturation operating point is generally unstable and the calculated low-frequency resistances become negative, indicating latch-like behavior.

In short, the simplest saturated model gives a current-to-voltage relationship controlled primarily by \(M_2\), with incremental transimpedance approximately \(1/g_{m2}\), but the regenerative-loop caveat is essential.

answer.text:
Assume both transistors are NMOS and the output is unloaded. Reading the mirrored symbol for \(M_2\) carefully:

\[
M_1:\quad G=X,\;D=V_{out},\;S=0,
\qquad
M_2:\quad G=V_{out},\;D=X,\;S=0 .
\]

Thus, the circuit consists of two inverting common-source stages connected in a feedback loop.

## 1. DC operating point

Let \(I_{IN}\) be the dc value of \(I_{in}\). Since MOS gate currents are zero,

\[
I_{D2}=I_{IN},
\qquad
I_{D1}=\frac{V_{DD}-V_{out}}{R_{D1}} .
\]

If both transistors are saturated and square-law behavior is assumed, with

\[
\beta_i=\mu_n C_{ox}\left(\frac WL\right)_i ,
\]

and channel-length modulation neglected,

\[
I_{IN}=\frac{\beta_2}{2}(V_{out}-V_T)^2 ,
\]

so

\[
\boxed{V_{out}=V_T+\sqrt{\frac{2I_{IN}}{\beta_2}}}
\]

and

\[
I_{D1}=\frac{V_{DD}-V_{out}}{R_{D1}},
\qquad
\boxed{V_X=V_T+\sqrt{\frac{2I_{D1}}{\beta_1}} } .
\]

The corresponding transconductances are

\[
g_{m1}=\sqrt{2\beta_1 I_{D1}},
\qquad
g_{m2}=\sqrt{2\beta_2 I_{IN}} .
\]

These expressions apply only if both devices remain on and saturated:

\[
V_X>V_T,\qquad V_{out}>V_T,
\]
\[
V_{out}\ge V_X-V_T \quad (M_1\text{ saturation}),
\]
\[
V_X\ge V_{out}-V_T \quad (M_2\text{ saturation}).
\]

A suitable nonzero dc input bias current is required; otherwise node \(X\) is not properly biased.

## 2. Low-frequency small-signal analysis

Let \(i_{in}\), \(v_x\), and \(v_{out}\) denote small-signal quantities. Define

\[
R_1=R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1}.
\]

At the output node,

\[
\frac{v_{out}}{R_1}+g_{m1}v_x=0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
v_{out}=-g_{m1}R_1v_x .
\]

At node \(X\),

\[
i_{in}=\frac{v_x}{r_{o2}}+g_{m2}v_{out}.
\]

Solving gives the transimpedance

\[
\boxed{
\frac{v_{out}}{i_{in}}
=
-\frac{g_{m1}R_1r_{o2}}{1-T_0}
}
\]

and the input resistance

\[
\boxed{
R_{in}\equiv\frac{v_x}{i_{in}}
=
\frac{r_{o2}}{1-T_0}
}
\]

where

\[
\boxed{
T_0=g_{m1}g_{m2}R_1r_{o2}
}
\]

is the low-frequency loop gain.

To find the output resistance, set the signal input current to zero—i.e., open-circuit the small-signal current source—and apply a test source at \(V_{out}\). Then

\[
v_x=-g_{m2}r_{o2}v_{out},
\]

which yields

\[
\boxed{
R_{out}=\frac{R_1}{1-T_0}
}.
\]

## 3. Feedback polarity and circuit behavior

The two stage gains are

\[
\frac{v_{out}}{v_x}=-g_{m1}R_1,
\qquad
\left.\frac{v_x}{v_{out}}\right|_{i_{in}=0}
=-g_{m2}r_{o2}.
\]

Their product is positive, so the circuit has **positive feedback**, not negative feedback. Qualitatively,

\[
V_X\uparrow
\Rightarrow I_{D1}\uparrow
\Rightarrow V_{out}\downarrow
\Rightarrow I_{D2}\downarrow ,
\]

and the resulting excess input current tends to raise \(V_X\) further.

Consequently:

- **\(T_0<1\):** \(R_{in}\) and \(R_{out}\) are positive. The transimpedance is negative, and positive feedback increases its magnitude.
- **\(T_0\to1\):** the ideal small-signal gain and resistances approach infinity.
- **\(T_0>1\):** the calculated resistances become negative. The saturation operating point is regenerative and generally metastable; the circuit can leave saturation and exhibit latch-like behavior, with cutoff/triode operation determining the final state.

In the formal limit \(r_{o1},r_{o2}\to\infty\), differentiation of the dc equations gives

\[
\frac{v_{out}}{i_{in}}=\frac1{g_{m2}},
\qquad
\frac{v_x}{i_{in}}
=-\frac{1}{g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}},
\]

but \(r_{o2}=\infty\) also implies \(T_0\to\infty\), so these relations do not by themselves guarantee a stable linear-amplifier operating point.

## 1. DC operating point

At DC, all of \(I_{\text{IN}}\) flows through \(M_2\), while \(M_1\) is supplied through \(R_{D1}\):

\[
I_{D2}=I_{\text{IN}},\qquad
I_{D1}=\frac{V_{DD}-V_{\text{OUT}}}{R_{D1}}.
\]

If both transistors are saturated and channel-length modulation is neglected, define

\[
k_i=\mu_n C_{\text{ox}}\left(\frac WL\right)_i .
\]

Then

\[
I_{\text{IN}}=\frac{k_2}{2}(V_{\text{OUT}}-V_{TH2})^2,
\]

so

\[
\boxed{V_{\text{OUT}}\simeq V_{TH2}+\sqrt{\frac{2I_{\text{IN}}}{k_2}}}
\]

and

\[
\boxed{
V_X\simeq V_{TH1}+
\sqrt{\frac{2(V_{DD}-V_{\text{OUT}})}{k_1R_{D1}}}
}.
\]

These equations assume the active operating branch; the saturation conditions are

\[
V_X\ge V_{\text{OUT}}-V_{TH2}\quad(M_2),
\qquad
V_{\text{OUT}}\ge V_X-V_{TH1}\quad(M_1).
\]

## 2. Low-frequency small-signal analysis

Let \(v_x\), \(v_o\), and \(i_{\text{in}}\) denote incremental quantities, with \(i_{\text{in}}\) entering node \(X\). Since \(V_{DD}\) is AC ground, define

\[
R_O=R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1}.
\]

The small-signal equations are:

- At the output node:
  \[
  g_{m1}v_x+\frac{v_o}{R_O}=0
  \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
  \boxed{\frac{v_o}{v_x}=-g_{m1}R_O}.
  \]

- At node \(X\), where \(V_{GS2}=v_o\) and \(V_{DS2}=v_x\):
  \[
  i_{\text{in}}=g_{m2}v_o+\frac{v_x}{r_{o2}}.
  \]

\[
\boxed{
\frac{v_o}{i_{\text{in}}}
=
\frac{-g_{m1}R_Or_{o2}}
{1-g_{m1}g_{m2}R_Or_{o2}}
}
\]

and

\[
\boxed{
R_{\text{in}}=\frac{v_x}{i_{\text{in}}}
=
\frac{r_{o2}}
{1-g_{m1}g_{m2}R_Or_{o2}}
}.
\]

The output resistance, measured with the ideal input current source set to zero (open-circuited for small signals), is

\[
\boxed{
R_{\text{out}}
=
\frac{R_O}
{1-g_{m1}g_{m2}R_Or_{o2}}
}.
\]

Thus the natural loop-gain parameter is

\[
\boxed{T=g_{m1}g_{m2}R_Or_{o2}}.
\]

## 3. Feedback polarity and important limit

The feedback is **positive voltage–current (shunt–shunt) feedback**. For example,

\[
v_o\uparrow
\;\Rightarrow\; I_{D2}\uparrow
\;\Rightarrow\; v_x\downarrow
\;\Rightarrow\; I_{D1}\downarrow
\;\Rightarrow\; v_o\uparrow .
\]

Hence the output perturbation reinforces itself.

For \(T<1\), positive feedback increases gain and both resistances by \(1/(1-T)\). At \(T=1\), the ideal low-frequency gain becomes unbounded. For \(T>1\), the expressions predict negative input/output resistances, and the active bias point is regenerative and unstable in the simplest two-node dynamic model.

If channel-length modulation is neglected entirely, \(r_{o2}\rightarrow\infty\), and the algebraic results reduce to

\[
\boxed{\frac{v_o}{i_{\text{in}}}=\frac{1}{g_{m2}}}
\]

and

\[
\boxed{
R_{\text{in}}=-\frac{1}{g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}}
}.
\]

The negative input resistance is a direct consequence of the positive feedback; consequently, the \(1/g_{m2}\) transimpedance result should not be interpreted as evidence of a stable linear amplifier without checking the loop gain and operating point.

- Both sources are grounded.

- Both drains are tied together at the output node **$V_{out}$**.
- $R_{D1}$ is the drain load resistor.
- $I_{in}$ is a current signal injected into the high-impedance gate node **X**.

## DC Operating Point

Assuming both devices operate in **saturation**:

$$V_{GS1} = V_{GS2} = V_X$$

$$I_{D1} = \frac{1}{2}\mu_n C_{ox}\left(\frac{W}{L}\right)_1 (V_X - V_{TH1})^2(1 + \lambda_1 V_{DS1})$$

$$I_{D2} = \frac{1}{2}\mu_n C_{ox}\left(\frac{W}{L}\right)_2 (V_X - V_{TH2})^2(1 + \lambda_2 V_{DS2})$$

The output DC voltage is:

$$\boxed{V_{out} = V_{DD} - (I_{D1} + I_{D2})R_{D1}}$$

*Note: In practice, node X needs a DC bias path (not shown) because the gate is DC-isolated from the current source.*

## Small-Signal Analysis

The small-signal model has:
- Two transconductance currents: $g_{m1}v_x$ and $g_{m2}v_x$, both pulling down on $V_{out}$
- Three parallel output resistances: $r_{o1} \parallel r_{o2} \parallel R_{D1}$

### Voltage Gain

$$\boxed{A_v = \frac{v_{out}}{v_x} = -(g_{m1} + g_{m2})(R_{D1} \parallel r_{o1} \parallel r_{o2})}$$

The negative sign indicates signal inversion.

### Input Resistance

At low frequencies, the gate resistance is essentially infinite:

$$\boxed{R_{in,X} \approx \infty}$$

### Output Resistance

$$\boxed{R_{out} = R_{D1} \parallel r_{o1} \parallel r_{o2}}$$

## Transimpedance with $I_{in}$

Since the gate draws negligible DC current, the current source $I_{in}$ drives the gate capacitance. The input capacitance at node X is dominated by:

$$C_{in} \approx C_{gs1} + C_{gs2} + C_{gd1}(1 + |A_v|) + C_{gd2}(1 + |A_v|)$$

where the $C_{gd}$ terms experience Miller multiplication.

For an ideal current source driving the gate:

$$v_x = \frac{i_{in}}{sC_{in}}$$

$$\boxed{Z_T(s) = \frac{v_{out}}{i_{in}} = \frac{-(g_{m1} + g_{m2})(R_{out})}{sC_{in}}}$$

This gives an integrating-type response with a pole at/near DC.

|---|---|
| **Topology** | Common-source, two parallel NMOS |
| **Voltage gain** | $A_v = -(g_{m1}+g_{m2})(R_{D1} \parallel r_{o1} \parallel r_{o2})$ |
| **Input resistance** | $\approx \infty$ |
| **Output resistance** | $R_{D1} \parallel r_{o1} \parallel r_{o2}$ |

I read the schematic as:

- \(M_1\) and \(M_2\) are **n‑channel** MOSFETs (sources grounded, arrows on the sources pointing to ground).
- \(M_1\) is a **common‑source** stage: gate \(=X\), drain \(=V_{\rm out}\), loaded by \(R_{D1}\).
- \(M_2\) is a **feedback** transistor: gate \(=V_{\rm out}\), drain \(=X\).
- The current source injects current into node \(X\).

Thus the two transistors are **cross‑coupled** (a single‑ended regenerative pair).

---

## 1. DC / large‑signal analysis

Assume both devices are in saturation and follow the long‑channel square law:

\[
I_D=\frac12 k(V_{GS}-V_{TH})^2
\]

The gate of \(M_1\) draws no DC current, so the entire source current flows through \(M_2\):

\[
I_{D2}=I_{\rm in}
\]

Since \(V_{GS2}=V_{\rm out}\),

\[
\boxed{
V_{\rm out}=V_{TH2}+\sqrt{\frac{2I_{\rm in}}{k_2}}
}
\tag{1}
\]

The current through \(M_1\) is set by the drop across \(R_{D1}\):

\[
I_{D1}=\frac{V_{DD}-V_{\rm out}}{R_{D1}}
=\frac12 k_1(V_X-V_{TH1})^2
\]

so

\[
\boxed{
V_X=V_{TH1}+\sqrt{\frac{2(V_{DD}-V_{\rm out})}{k_1R_{D1}}}
}
\tag{2}
\]

Saturation requires

\[
V_{\rm out}\ge V_X-V_{TH1},\qquad
V_X\ge V_{\rm out}-V_{TH2}.
\]

Note that \(I_{\rm in}>0\) is required; if \(I_{\rm in}\) is purely AC, a DC bias path must be provided.

---

## 2. Small‑signal low‑frequency analysis

Let lowercase symbols denote small signals and define

\[
g_{m1}=k_1(V_X-V_{TH1}),\qquad
g_{m2}=k_2(V_{\rm out}-V_{TH2}).
\]

Sources are AC ground, so

\[
v_{gs1}=v_x,\qquad v_{gs2}=v_o .
\]

### Node \(X\)

The gate of \(M_1\) is an open circuit, so the injected current must exit through \(M_2\):

\[
i_{\rm in}=g_{m2}v_o
\]

Hence the **transimpedance** is

\[
\boxed{
A_Z=\frac{v_o}{i_{\rm in}}=\frac{1}{g_{m2}}
}
\tag{3}
\]

### Output node

\[
\frac{v_o}{R_{D1}}+g_{m1}v_x=0
\]

so the voltage gain of \(M_1\) is

\[
\boxed{
\frac{v_o}{v_x}=-g_{m1}R_{D1}
}
\tag{4}
\]

and

\[
v_x=-\frac{v_o}{g_{m1}R_{D1}}
=-\frac{i_{\rm in}}{g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}}.
\]

Therefore the **incremental resistance seen at node \(X\)** is

\[
\boxed{
R_{\rm in}=\frac{v_x}{i_{\rm in}}
=-\frac{1}{g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}}
}
\tag{5}
\]

It is **negative** because the loop is regenerative.

---

## 3. Including channel‑length modulation

Let \(r_{o1},r_{o2}\) be finite and define

\[
R_L=R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1}.
\]

The nodal equations become

\[
i_{\rm in}=g_{m2}v_o+\frac{v_x}{r_{o2}},
\]

\[
\frac{v_o}{R_L}+g_{m1}v_x=0
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
v_x=-\frac{v_o}{g_{m1}R_L}.
\]

Solving,

\[
\boxed{
Z_T=\frac{v_o}{i_{\rm in}}
=\frac{1}{\,g_{m2}-\dfrac{1}{g_{m1}r_{o2}R_L}\,}
\approx\frac{1}{g_{m2}}
}
\tag{6}
\]

\[
\boxed{
R_{\rm in}
=-\frac{1}{g_{m1}R_L\left(g_{m2}-\dfrac{1}{g_{m1}r_{o2}R_L}\right)}
\approx -\frac{1}{g_{m1}g_{m2}R_L}
}
\tag{7}
\]

The **output resistance** (looking into \(V_{\rm out}\) with \(i_{\rm in}=0\)) is

\[
\boxed{
R_{\rm out}
=\frac{1}{\,\dfrac{1}{R_L}-g_{m1}g_{m2}r_{o2}\,}
}
\tag{8}
\]

which can also be negative.

---

## 4. Interpretation

- The circuit converts an input current at node \(X\) into an output voltage with a small‑signal transimpedance of approximately \(1/g_{m2}\).
- Because \(M_1\) inverts and \(M_2\) returns current to the same node, the feedback is **positive**.
- Consequently, the incremental resistances at \(X\) and at \(V_{\rm out}\) are **negative**.
- The cell is therefore a **regenerative / negative‑resistance circuit** rather than a simple stable amplifier. It can be used as an active negative resistance (e.g. in oscillators or regenerative amplifiers), but it can latch or oscillate if the loop gain is too large.
