answer.text:
Both devices are NMOS, with source and bulk to ground,
so there is no body effect. The connections are

$$
\begin{array}{c|ccc}
 & G & D & S\\ \hline
M_{1}&X&V_{out}&0\\
M_{2}&V_{out}&X&0
\end{array}
$$

i.e. the gate of each is tied to the drain of the other.
It is a cross-coupled pair with very asymmetric drain loads:
$R_{D1}$ in $M_{1}$ and the (ideal) current source $I_{in}$
in $M_{2}$. It is a regenerative, positive feedback cell --
in essence a MOS latch / negative resistance cell, not a
conventional linear amplifier.

### 1.  Formal d-c solution in saturation

Gate currents are zero, so KCL at $X$ gives, in any
finite d-c equilibrium,

$$
I_{D2}=I_{in}\tag{1}
$$

and at the output

$$
I_{D1}=\frac{V_{DD}-V_{out}}{R_{D1}} .\tag{2}
$$

With $k_{ni}=\mu_nC_{ox}(W/L)_i$, $\lambda\ne0$ in general,

$$\begin{aligned}
I_{in}&=\tfrac{k_{n2}}2\,(V_{out}-V_{th})^{2}(1+\lambda V_X)\\
\frac{V_{DD}-V_{out}}{R_{D1}}&=
 \tfrac{k_{n1}}2\,(V_{X}-V_{th})^{2}(1+\lambda V_{out}) .
\end{aligned}\tag{3}$$

For $\lambda\to0$ this decouples,

$$
\,V_{out}\approx V_{th}+\sqrt{\frac{2I_{in}}{k_{n2}}}\,,\qquad
\,V_{X}\approx V_{th}+\sqrt{\frac{2I_{D1}}{k_{n1}}}\,,\qquad
I_{D1}=\frac{V_{DD}-V_{out}}{R_{D1}}  \tag{4}
$$

with saturation requiring
$V_{out}\ge V_X-V_{th}$, $V_X\ge V_{out}-V_{th}$.
A SPICE operating point will often find (3)-(4).  It is,
however, unstable, as shown next.

### 2.  Small signals, loop gain

Let $C_X$ be the capacitance at $X$
($C_{gs1}+C_{db2}+\dots$) and $C_O$ at the output
($C_{gs2}+C_{db1}+\dots$).  With
$g_{mi},\,r_{oi}$ at the point (4),

$$\begin{aligned}
(sC_X+g_{o2})v_x+g_{m2}v_{out}&=i_{in}\\
g_{m1}v_x+(sC_O+G_D)v_{out}&=0
\end{aligned}\qquad 
G_D\equiv\frac1{R_{D1}}+\frac1{r_{o1}},\;\;g_{o2}=\frac1{r_{o2}} \tag{5}$$

Breaking the loop at the gate of $M_{1}$ (node $X$):
$M_{1}$ is a common-source stage,
$v_{out}/v_x=-g_{m1}(R_{D1}\!\parallel\! r_{o1})$;
$M_{2}$ is a second common-source stage returning a
signal to $X$ with gain $-g_{m2}r_{o2}$.  Hence

$$
L(s)=\frac{g_{m1}g_{m2}}
{(sC_X+g_{o2})(sC_O+G_D)},\qquad 
L(0)=g_{m1}g_{m2}r_{o2}\bigl(R_{D1}\!\parallel\! r_{o1}\bigr)>0 \tag{6}
$$

Two inversions make the feedback positive, and normally
$L(0)\gg1$ since it is the product of two intrinsic
stage gains.

Formally, from (5),

$$
\frac{v_{out}}{i_{in}}=
\frac{1}{\,g_{m2}-\dfrac{1}{g_{m1}r_{o2}(R_{D1}\!\parallel\! r_{o1})}\,}
\;\approx\;\frac{1}{g_{m2}}\frac{1}{1-1/L(0)}
\;\approx\;\frac1{g_{m2}} \tag{7}
$$

but this is the (differential) slope of the unstable
branch (3).  The characteristic equation $1-L(s)=0$ is

$$
(sC_X+g_{o2})(sC_O+G_D)-g_{m1}g_{m2}=0, \tag{8}
$$

whose constant term $g_{o2}G_D-g_{m1}g_{m2}<0$ for $L(0)>1$.
Hence one pole is in the right half plane, approximately

$$
s_{+}\approx
\frac{g_{m1}g_{m2}-g_{o2}G_D}{C_XG_D+C_Og_{o2}}>0,
$$

and the saturated bias point repels transients
regeneratively, with time constant $\approx 1/s_{+}$,
until a device leaves saturation.

### 3.  Negative port resistances

Apply a test voltage at the output with $i_{in}=0$ (a-c).
KCL at the floating node $X$ gives $g_{m2}v_{out}+v_x/r_{o2}=0$,
i.e. $v_x=-g_{m2}r_{o2}v_{out}$.  Thus

$$
R_{out}=\frac{v_{out}}{i_t}
=\left[\frac1{R_{D1}}+\frac1{r_{o1}}-g_{m1}g_{m2}r_{o2}\right]^{-1}
\;\approx\;-\,\frac{1}{g_{m1}g_{m2}r_{o2}}\;<\;0 . \tag{9}
$$

Similarly, looking into node $X$ with the output
terminated in $R_{D1}$,

$$
R_{X}= \left[\frac1{r_{o2}}-g_{m1}g_{m2}
\bigl(R_{D1}\!\parallel\! r_{o1}\bigr)\right]^{-1}
\approx -\frac{1}{g_{m1}g_{m2}(R_{D1}\!\parallel\! r_{o1})}<0 . \tag{10}
$$

$g_{m2}$ is set by the bias $I_{D2}=I_{in}$,
$g_{m2}\approx\sqrt{2k_{n2}I_{in}}$, and $g_{m1}$ by
$I_{D1}$ in (2), so $I_{in}$ controls $|R_{out}|$.
With an $LC$ tank at $V_{out}$ this negative resistance
can cancel the tank loss, $|R_{out}|<R_{p,\text{tank}}$,
giving a (nonlinearly amplitude-limited) oscillator;
without a tank it simply latches.

### 4.  Large-signal behaviour

The physically stable high state is

* $M_{1}$ essentially off, $M_{2}$ on in triode,
* $V_{out}\approx V_{DD}$ (no drop in $R_{D1}$),
* $I_{in}=k_{n2}\!\left[(V_{DD}-V_{th})V_X-V_X^{2}/2\right]$,
  $V_X$ small, $V_X<V_{th1}$.

Here $g_{m1}\approx0$, the loop is open, and the state is
stable.  As $I_{in}$ (or a disturbance at $X$) raises
$V_X$ toward $V_{th1}$, $M_{1}$ turns on, $V_{out}$ falls,
$M_{2}$ must raise $V_X$ further to keep carrying
$I_{in}$, and the loop gain passes through unity:
snap-action.  The trigger current is of the order of
$I_{D2}$ evaluated at $V_X\!\approx\! V_{th1}$, $V_{GS2}=V_{DD}$,

$$
I_{\text{trig}}\;\sim\;
k_{n2}\Bigl[(V_{DD}-V_{th})V_{th}-\tfrac12V_{th}^{2}\Bigr].
$$

After triggering, $M_{2}$ is off, $M_{1}$ is on in triode
carrying $\approx V_{DD}/R_{D1}$, $V_{out}\approx0$;
in the ideal model $V_X$ then runs to the compliance of
the $I_{in}$ source (in practice limited by the source,
leakage or breakdown, and a reset device is normally
added to discharge $X$).  The saturated point (4) is
the separatrix between the two basins.

In short: $M_{1}$-$M_{2}$ is a positive-feedback
cross-coupled latch presenting
$R_{out}\approx-1/g_{m1}g_{m2}r_{o2}$ at its output.
It is usable as a regenerative current-threshold
detector/sense amplifier and as a negative-resistance
oscillator cell, but the all-saturated operating point
(4) with formal transresistance $\approx1/g_{m2}$ is
unstable for the usual $g_{m1}g_{m2}r_{o2}(R_{D1}\!\parallel\!r_{o1})\gg1$.

answer.text:
The two devices are NMOS, sources and bodies to ground.
$$
M_{1}: G=X,\;D=V_{out},\;S=0\qquad 
M_{2}: G=V_{out},\;D=X,\;S=0
$$
i.e. the gate of each is the drain of the other.  $M_{1}$ is a
common-source device with load $R_{D1}$; the drain of $M_{2}$ is
loaded by the (high impedance) current source $I_{in}$.
It is a cross coupled, positive feedback, pair - in ordinary
sizes a latch, not a stable linear transimpedance amplifier.

Let $\beta_i=\mu_nC_{ox}(W/L)_i$, $V_{TH}$ the (common) threshold,
$\lambda =0$ for the essentials.  Gate currents are zero, so in
any internal d-c equilibrium

$$\;I_{in}=I_{D2}\;\qquad 
V_{out}=V_{DD}-I_{D1}R_{D1} \tag{1}$$

$$ 
I_{D1}= \tfrac{\beta_1}{2}(V_X-V_{TH})^{2}\;\;{\rm sat.},\qquad
I_{D2}= \beta_{2}\!\left[(V_{out}-V_{TH})V_X-\tfrac12V_X^{2}\right]\;\;{\rm lin.\;etc.}
$$

### The $I$--$V$ seen at $X$

Let $I_X=I_{D2}$ be the current the $M_1M_2R_{D1}$ network sinks
from node $X$, $V_{out}$ being allowed to follow $V_X$ through
$M_1,R_{D1}$.

* $V_X<V_{TH}$: $M_1$ off, $V_{out}=V_{DD}$, $M_2$ in the linear
region with $V_{GS2}=V_{DD}$,
$$
I_X=\beta_2\big[(V_{DD}-V_{TH})V_X-\tfrac12V_X^{2}\big],\qquad 
\frac{dI_X}{dV_X}>0 .
$$

* $V_X>V_{TH}$: $M_1$ turns on,
$$
V_{out}\approx V_{DD}-\frac{\beta_1R_{D1}}2\,(V_X-V_{TH})^{2}
\tag{2}$$
falls, hence $V_{GS2}=V_{out}$ falls.  With $M_2$ still
essentially linear,
$$
I_X=\beta_2\big[(V_{out}(V_X)-V_{TH})V_X-\tfrac12V_X^{2}\big].
$$
$I_X(V_X)$ rises, reaches a maximum, and then falls to
$\approx0$ when $V_{out}<V_{TH}$ turns $M_2$ off.  It is a
voltage controlled negative differential resistance
characteristic

```
 Ix ^          I_T+
    |           /\
    |          /  \   dIx/dVx < 0 : unstable
    |         /    \____  M2 off
    |        /
    +------------------------> Vx
                 VTH
```

A horizontal load line $I_X=I_{in}$ intersects the rising part
in a stable point, the falling part in an unstable point.
For $I_{in}$ larger than the peak there is no internal
intersection at all.

Indeed, about a both-on saturated point, with $C_X,C_{out}$
the node capacitances,

$$\begin{aligned}
C_X\dot v_x&=-g_{ds2}v_x-g_{m2}v_{out}\\
C_{out}\dot v_{out}&=-g_{m1}v_x-\big(R_{D1}^{-1}+g_{ds1}\big)v_{out}
\end{aligned}\qquad 
v_{out}=-g_{m1}(R_{D1}\!\parallel r_{o1})v_x $$

The (positive) loop gain round $v_x\to v_{out}\to i_{d2}\to v_x$ is

$$
\,T=g_{m1}(R_{D1}\!\parallel r_{o1})\;g_{m2}r_{o2}\,>0
$$

$v_x\uparrow\;\Rightarrow\;v_{out}\downarrow\;\Rightarrow\;
i_{d2}\downarrow\;\Rightarrow\;v_x\uparrow$ still more.
Formally

$$
\frac{v_{out}}{i_{in}}=
\frac{-\,g_{m1}(R_{D1}\!\parallel r_{o1})}
{\,r_{o2}^{-1}-g_{m1}g_{m2}(R_{D1}\!\parallel r_{o1})\,}
\approx\frac1{g_{m2}},\qquad
R_{X}\equiv\frac{v_x}{i_{in}}=
\frac{r_{o2}}{1-T}\approx
-\,\frac{1}{g_{m1}g_{m2}(R_{D1}\!\parallel r_{o1})}\;\;{\rm for}\;T\gg1,
$$

i.e. a negative resistance at $X$.  For $T<1$ this would be a
stable positive-feedback amplifier of enhanced gain $ \propto
1/(1-T)$; in practice $g_mr_o\gg1$ and $T\gg1$, the both-on
point, e.g.
$V_{out}=V_{TH}+\sqrt{2I_{in}/\beta_2}$,
$V_X=V_{TH}+\sqrt{2(V_{DD}-V_{out})/\beta_1R_{D1}}$, is a saddle,
unobservable in steady state.

### The two usable states

1. Output high.  $M_1$ (essentially) off, $M_2$ on, linear:
$$
V_{out}\approx V_{DD},\qquad 
I_{in}= \beta_2\big[(V_{DD}-V_{TH})V_X-\tfrac12V_X^{2}\big],
$$
$V_X$ small.  Stable while the loop gain on this branch is
$<1$.

2. Output low, railed.  $V_{out}$ has been driven below
$V_{TH}$, $M_2$ is off, $M_1$ is hard on.  In the ideal model
$V_X$ is driven to the compliance limit $V_{X,\max}$ of the
$I_{in}$ source ($\sim V_{DD}$ in practice), and, with $M_1$
in the linear region,
$$
\frac{V_{DD}-V_{out,L}}{R_{D1}}\approx
\beta_1\big[(V_{X,\max}-V_{TH})V_{out,L}-\tfrac12V_{out,L}^{2}\big]
\;\;\approx\;\;
\frac{V_{DD}}{1+\beta_1R_{D1}(V_{X,\max}-V_{TH})}\ll V_{DD}.
$$
The loop is opened by $M_2$ being off.

### Trip current

To first order regeneration starts when $V_X$ reaches
$V_{TH1}$ with $V_{out}\approx V_{DD}$, i.e. for $V_{DD}>2V_{TH}$

$$
\,I_{T+}\;\approx\;I_{D2}\big|_{V_{GS}=V_{DD},\,V_{DS}=V_{TH}}
      =\beta_{2}V_{TH}\Bigl(V_{DD}-\tfrac32V_{TH}\Bigr)\,  .
$$

Exactly, in the square law model, the trip is the peak of
$I_X(V_X)$, $dI_X/dV_X=0$, i.e. $T=1$ on the high branch:
with (2), in the linear-$M_2$/saturated-$M_1$ region,
$$
V_{out,T}-V_{TH}-V_{X,T}=R_{D1}\,\beta_1(V_{X,T}-V_{TH})V_{X,T},
\qquad 
I_{T+}= \beta_2\big[(V_{out,T}-V_{TH})V_{X,T}-\tfrac12V_{X,T}^{2}\big].
$$
Increasing $\beta_2$ raises $I_{T+}$; increasing $\beta_1$ or
$R_{D1}$ makes $V_{out}$ fall faster, strengthens the feedback
and lowers $I_{T+}$.  Once past the peak,
$v_x$ grows essentially exponentially: $M_1$ pulls $V_{out}$
down, $M_2$ sinks less and less of $I_{in}$, $V_X$ rises
further, until $M_2$ is off and $V_{out}$ is low.  Pulling
$V_X$ back down, by a reset device or by an $I_{in}$ that can
sink current, until $V_{out}(V_X)$ rises to $V_{TH2}$,
turns $M_2$ on and regenerates in the opposite direction.

In short: a regenerative NMOS latch / current-mode trip
circuit, presenting a negative resistance at $X$, with a
high output $\approx V_{DD}$ for $I_{in}<I_{T+}$ and a latched
low output for $I_{in}>I_{T+}$.  It is used, with an explicit
reset, as a current comparator, latch/sense element and
negative-resistance element; with only a unidirectional
ideal $I_{in}$ it trips once and must be reset externally.

M1 and $M_{2}$ are NMOS devices with source and bulk to ground,
hence with no body effect.

$$\begin{aligned}
M_{1}:&\qquad G=X,\quad D=V_{out},\quad S=0\\
M_{2}:&\qquad G=V_{out},\quad D=X,\quad S=0
\end{aligned}$$

$M_{1}$ is a common source stage $X\to V_{out}$ with load $R_{D1}$.
$M_{2}$ is a common source stage $V_{out}\to X$ whose drain load
is, ideally, the input current source.  Two inverting stages are
connected in a ring: it is a regenerative, i.e. positive feedback,
circuit.

### DC, formal

Gate currents are zero, so at $X$ and at the output

$$ I_{D2}=I_{in},\qquad 
I_{D1}=\frac{V_{DD}-V_{out}}{R_{D1}} \tag{1}$$

with, in saturation and $\beta_i=\mu_nC_{ox}(W/L)_i$,

$$\begin{aligned}
I_{D2}&=\tfrac12\beta_2\,(V_{out}-V_{TH})^{2}(1+\lambda V_X)\\
I_{D1}&=\tfrac12\beta_1\,(V_{X}-V_{TH})^{2}(1+\lambda V_{out}) .
\end{aligned}$$

For $\lambda\approx0$

$$ V_{out}\approx V_{TH}+\sqrt{\frac{2I_{in}}{\beta_2}},\qquad
V_{X}\approx V_{TH}+\sqrt{\frac{2I_{D1}}{\beta_1}},\qquad
I_{D1}= \frac{V_{DD}-V_{out}}{R_{D1}} .$$

$M_{2}$ must take exactly $I_{in}$; $V_{out}$ is essentially the
$V_{GS2}$ needed to do so.  $M_{1}$ and $R_{D1}$ must then produce
that $V_{out}$, which fixes $V_X=V_{GS1}$.  Both saturated requires

$$V_{out}\ge V_X-V_{TH},\qquad V_X\ge V_{out}-V_{TH}.$$

### Small signal

Put $v_{gs1}=v_x$, $v_{gs2}=v_{out}$.  KCL at $X$ and at the output,
with $R'\equiv R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1}$, is

$$\begin{aligned}
i_{in}&=g_{m2}v_{out}+\frac{v_x}{r_{o2}} &&\text{at }X \tag{2}\\
0&=g_{m1}v_x+v_{out}\!\left(\frac1{R_{D1}}+\frac1{r_{o1}}\right)
   &&\text{at }V_{out} \tag{3}
\end{aligned}$$

From (3) the $M_{1}$ stage gain is

$$\frac{v_{out}}{v_x}=-g_{m1}R'=-g_{m1}(R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1}) .$$

Solving (2)-(3),

$$\,R_m\equiv\frac{v_{out}}{i_{in}}
      =\frac{1}{\,g_{m2}-\dfrac{1}{g_{m1}R'r_{o2}}\,}\,  \tag{4}$$

$$\,R_{in}\equiv\frac{v_x}{i_{in}}
      =\frac{1}{\,1/r_{o2}-g_{m1}g_{m2}R'\,}
      =-\frac{1}{g_{m1}g_{m2}R'-1/r_{o2}}\,  \tag{5}$$

i.e. for $r_o\to\infty$

$$\frac{v_{out}}{i_{in}}\approx\frac1{g_{m2}},\qquad
      \frac{v_x}{i_{in}}\approx-\frac{1}{g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}}<0 .$$

The input resistance at $X$ is negative.  Physically, a larger
$I_{in}$ requires a larger $V_{GS2}=V_{out}$.  To obtain a larger
$V_{out}$, $M_{1}$ must conduct less through $R_{D1}$, so $V_X$
must fall: $dV_X/dI_{in}<0$.

The resistance at the output, $i_{in}=0$ (a.c.) and $R_{D1}$
included, is likewise

$$R_{out}=
\frac{1}{\;1/R_{D1}+1/r_{o1}-g_{m1}g_{m2}r_{o2}\;}
\approx -\frac{1}{g_{m1}g_{m2}r_{o2}}<0 .$$

### Loop gain and stability

Breaking the loop at the gate of $M_{2}$,

$$L = \bigl(g_{m1}R'\bigr)\bigl(g_{m2}r_{o2}\bigr)>0,$$

the product of the two (negative) stage gains.
With capacitances $C_X,C_{out}$ the linearised characteristic
equation is, in essence,
$(sC_X+1/r_{o2})(sC_{out}+1/R')-g_{m1}g_{m2}=0$.
Its determinant is negative, i.e. there is a right-half-plane
pole, when

$$L=g_{m1}g_{m2}(R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1})r_{o2}>1,$$

which is normally true, since $g_mr_o\gg1$.  Hence the
both-saturated operating point above is the metastable point
of a latch, not a stable linear operating point.  The circuit
regenerates to e.g. $V_{out}\approx V_{DD}$, $V_X\approx0$,
$M_{1}$ off, $M_{2}$ in triode sinking $I_{in}$; the opposite
state is reached with a real, supply-limited $I_{in}$ source
clamping $V_X$ high and $V_{out}$ low.

In short: formally a transimpedance $v_{out}/i_{in}\approx1/g_{m2}$
with a small negative input (and output) resistance
$-1/g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}$.  With normal intrinsic gains
it is a positive-feedback latch / negative-resistance element,
useful for regeneration, hysteresis and oscillation, and usable
as a linear amplifier only if the loop gain is made $<1$, e.g.
by a sufficiently low shunt resistance at node $X$.

The schematic is nothing more exotic than a one–transistor current mirror (M2 is the sensing/diode device, M1 is the output device) that drives a load-resistor, RD1.  
The mirror converts the input current Iin into a current n·Iin ( n = (W/L)1 ⁄ (W/L)2 ) and that current is then converted into a voltage across RD1, so the whole block behaves as a simple trans-impedance amplifier.

Assumptions used below  
• Long-channel MOSFETs, square-law model, channel-length-modulation neglected unless stated.  
• All devices are NMOS, body tied to 0 V.  
• M1 and M2 operate in saturation.  

1. Node X voltage (large-signal)  
The input current is forced into the diode-connected transistor M2, therefore

 Iin = ID2 = ½ kn (W/L)2 (Vx – VTH)²     (1)

⇒ Vx = VTH + √[ 2 Iin / (kn (W/L)2) ]    (2)

2. Mirror action  
The same gate voltage Vx appears on M1, so (still neglecting λ)

 ID1 = ½ kn (W/L)1 (Vx – VTH)²  
   = (W/L)1 ⁄ (W/L)2 · Iin ≜ n Iin      (3)

Thus the mirror ratio n = (W/L)1/(W/L)2 sets how much of the input current is reproduced by M1.

3. Output voltage (large-signal)  
KCL at node Vout gives

 (VDD – Vout)/RD1 = ID1 = n Iin       (4)

⇒ Vout = VDD – n Iin RD1         (5)

Equation (5) is the DC transfer characteristic.  
The polarity is inverting: a positive input current drives the output voltage downward.

### 1. Circuit Identification and Topology
The circuit consists of the following components:

*   **Load Resistor:** $R_{D1}$ connected between $V_{DD}$ and the output node.
*   **Transistors:** Two NMOS transistors, $M_1$ and $M_2$.

**Topology Summary:**
Transistors $M_1$ and $M_2$ are connected in **parallel**. Their gates are tied together at node **X**, their sources are tied to ground, and their drains are tied together at the output node **$V_{out}$**. This configuration effectively creates a single equivalent transistor with a combined transconductance. The circuit is a **Common-Source amplifier** stage with a resistive load, driven by a current input.

### 2. DC Analysis
In a DC steady state, the gate current of a MOSFET is ideally zero ($I_G = 0$).
*   The input current source $I_{in}$ is connected to the gate node **X**. Since there is no DC path for the current to flow into the high-impedance gate (assuming ideal MOSFETs), the voltage at node **X** ($V_X$) would theoretically rise indefinitely until the transistors saturate or the supply limits are reached.
*   This implies that the circuit is intended to be analyzed as a **dynamic circuit** (transient response) or a **small-signal circuit** (AC analysis), rather than a simple DC bias circuit. It acts as an **integrator** or a **charge amplifier**.

If we assume a small leakage current or a bias mechanism exists to set the DC operating point:
*   The current flowing through $R_{D1}$ is the sum of the drain currents of $M_1$ and $M_2$: $I_{total} = I_{D1} + I_{D2}$.
*   The output voltage is given by: $V_{out} = V_{DD} - (I_{D1} + I_{D2})R_{D1}$.
*   Since $V_{GS1} = V_{GS2} = V_X$, the transistors share the current based on their aspect ratios ($W/L$).

### 3. Small-Signal Analysis
Let's analyze the circuit for small signals (AC analysis). Let $v_x$ be the small-signal voltage at node X and $v_{out}$ be the small-signal voltage at the output.

**A. Transistor Model:**
Since $M_1$ and $M_2$ are in parallel with sources grounded:
*   $v_{gs1} = v_x$
*   $v_{gs2} = v_x$
*   The total small-signal drain current generated by the transistors is $i_d = g_{m1}v_x + g_{m2}v_x = (g_{m1} + g_{m2})v_x$. Let $g_m = g_{m1} + g_{m2}$.
*   The output resistance of the transistors is $r_o = r_{o1} || r_{o2}$.

**B. Output Node ($V_{out}$):**
Applying Kirchhoff's Current Law (KCL) at the output node (setting $V_{DD}$ to AC ground):
The current flowing down from the output node through the parallel combination of $R_{D1}$, $r_{o1}$, and $r_{o2}$ must equal the current generated by the transistors.
$$ \frac{v_{out}}{R_{D1} || r_{o1} || r_{o2}} = - (g_{m1} + g_{m2}) v_x $$
Let $R_{out} = R_{D1} || r_{o1} || r_{o2}$.
$$ v_{out} = -g_m R_{out} v_x $$
This shows that the circuit is an **inverting amplifier** with voltage gain $A_v = -g_m R_{out}$.

**C. Input Node (X):**
The input current $i_{in}$ flows into node X. Since the gate impedance is infinite at low frequencies, the current flows into the parasitic capacitances at the gate.
*   Capacitances to ground: $C_{gs1}, C_{gs2}$.
*   Capacitances to output (feedback): $C_{gd1}, C_{gd2}$.

Applying KCL at node X:
$$ i_{in} = s C_{gs1} v_x + s C_{gd1} (v_x - v_{out}) + s C_{gs2} v_x + s C_{gd2} (v_x - v_{out}) $$
$$ i_{in} = s (C_{gs1} + C_{gs2} + C_{gd1} + C_{gd2}) v_x - s (C_{gd1} + C_{gd2}) v_{out} $$

Substituting $v_{out} = -g_m R_{out} v_x$:
$$ i_{in} = s [ (C_{gs1} + C_{gs2}) + (C_{gd1} + C_{gd2})(1 + g_m R_{out}) ] v_x $$

This term in the brackets is the effective input capacitance, $C_{in}$, which includes the **Miller Effect** multiplication of the gate-drain capacitance.
$$ C_{in} \approx C_{gs} + C_{gd}(1 + |A_v|) $$
where $C_{gs} = C_{gs1} + C_{gs2}$ and $C_{gd} = C_{gd1} + C_{gd2}$.

So, $v_x = \frac{i_{in}}{s C_{in}}$.

**D. Transfer Function:**
Combining the equations:
$$ v_{out} = -g_m R_{out} v_x = -g_m R_{out} \left( \frac{i_{in}}{s C_{in}} \right) $$
$$ \frac{V_{out}(s)}{I_{in}(s)} = - \frac{g_m R_{out}}{s C_{in}} $$

### 4. Conclusion and Function
*   **Circuit Function:** This circuit acts as a **Transimpedance Integrator** (or Charge Amplifier). It converts an input current $I_{in}$ into an output voltage $V_{out}$.
*   **Gain:** The transfer function is $Z_t(s) = \frac{V_{out}}{I_{in}} = \frac{-g_m R_{out}}{s C_{in}}$. The magnitude of the transimpedance gain decreases with frequency (roll-off of -20 dB/decade), characteristic of an integrator.
*   **Phase:** The output is inverted (180-degree phase shift) relative to the input current integration.
*   **Bandwidth:** The bandwidth is limited by the Miller capacitance. The unity-gain frequency (where $|V_{out}/I_{in}| = 1 \Omega$) is approximately $\omega_{UG} = \frac{g_m R_{out}}{C_{in}}$.

In summary, the parallel transistors $M_1$ and $M_2$ increase the total transconductance ($g_m$) and drive strength, while the resistor $R_{D1}$ sets the output impedance and DC gain factor. The lack of a feedback resistor from output to input makes it an integrator.

    *   **Source**: Connected to node $X$ (top terminal, higher potential). *Note: In standard PMOS operation for this feedback loop to work, the source must be at the higher potential node $X$.*
    *   **Drain/Body**: Connected to ground (bottom terminal).
    *   **Function**: Acts as a voltage-controlled current sink. It draws current from node $X$ to ground, controlled by the output voltage $V_{\text{out}}$.
*   **$I_{\text{in}}$**: Input current source driving node $X$.

### 3. Circuit Operation (DC Analysis)
The circuit operates based on the balance of currents at node $X$ and the feedback loop.

1.  **Input Stage**: The input current $I_{\text{in}}$ flows into node $X$. Since the gate of $M_1$ draws negligible DC current, this current must flow through transistor $M_2$ to ground.
    $$I_{\text{in}} \approx I_{D2}$$
    (Current through $M_2$)

2.  **Feedback Mechanism**:
    *   $M_2$ is a PMOS transistor with its gate at $V_{\text{out}}$ and source at $X$. The source-gate voltage is $V_{SG2} = V_X - V_{\text{out}}$.
    *   The current through $M_2$ is approximately: $I_{D2} = \frac{1}{2} k_{p2} (V_{SG2} - |V_{thp}|)^2 = \frac{1}{2} k_{p2} (V_X - V_{\text{out}} - |V_{thp}|)^2$.
    *   Since $I_{\text{in}} = I_{D2}$, the input current determines the relationship between $V_X$ and $V_{\text{out}}$.

    *   $M_1$ (NMOS) is in saturation (assuming proper biasing). Its drain current is $I_{D1} = \frac{1}{2} k_{n1} (V_X - V_{thn})^2$.
    *   The output voltage is determined by the voltage drop across $R_{D1}$:
        $$V_{\text{out}} = V_{DD} - I_{D1} R_{D1}$$

**Stability (Negative Feedback Loop):**
*   Suppose $V_{\text{out}}$ decreases (e.g., due to a disturbance).
*   Since $M_2$ is a PMOS with Gate at $V_{\text{out}}$, a decrease in $V_{\text{out}}$ increases $V_{SG2} = V_X - V_{\text{out}}$.

*   This confirms **negative feedback**, making the circuit stable.

### 4. Small-Signal Analysis
We can determine the transimpedance gain ($v_{\text{out}} / i_{\text{in}}$).

*   For $M_1$ (Common Source): $v_{\text{out}} = -g_{m1} v_x R_{D1}$ (ignoring output resistance $r_{o1}$).

*   For $M_2$ (PMOS feedback element): The small signal current $i_{d2}$ flowing from $X$ to ground is:

    *   $v_{sg2} = v_x - v_{\text{out}}$
    *   $v_{sd2} = v_x - 0 = v_x$

Substituting $v_x$:

The transimpedance gain is:
$$ \frac{v_{\text{out}}}{i_{\text{in}}} \approx -\frac{1}{g_{m2}} $$
(Assuming $g_{m1} R_{D1} \gg 1$, which is typical for amplifiers).

### Conclusion
The circuit is an **inverting transimpedance amplifier**.
*   **Function**: Converts input current $I_{\text{in}}$ to output voltage $V_{\text{out}}$.
*   **Gain**: Approximately $-1/g_{m2}$ (where $g_{m2}$ is the transconductance of transistor $M_2$).

    *   If the voltage at node $X$ ($V_{GS1}$) **increases**, the current $I_{D1}$ increases.

*   **Stage 2 ($M_2$):** This acts as a common-source stage where the input is at the gate ($V_{out}$) and the output is at the drain (Node $X$). The load is the current source $I_{in}$ (which has high impedance).
    *   If $V_{out}$ ($V_{GS2}$) **increases**, the transistor $M_2$ turns on harder and draws more current ($I_{D2}$).

*   **Loop Gain**: The total loop gain is the product of the two stages: $A_{loop} = A_1 \times A_2 = (-) \times (-) = (+)$.
    *   Since the loop gain is positive, the circuit employs **positive feedback**.

### 3. Circuit Function
Circuits with positive feedback and high gain typically act as **bistable multivibrators (latches)** or **Schmitt triggers**. This circuit has two stable operating states and one unstable (metastable) state. It will "latch" into one of the two stable states depending on initial conditions or noise.

    *   As $V_X$ rises above the threshold voltage $V_{TH1}$, $M_1$ turns ON strongly.
    *   $M_1$ acts as a low resistance path to ground, pulling $V_{out}$ down towards 0 V.
    *   **This state is consistent and stable.** (Note: In a real circuit, $V_X$ would rise until limited by leakage or breakdown, keeping $M_1$ fully on).

**Metastable Point (Unstable Equilibrium)**
There is a theoretical DC operating point where both transistors are in saturation.
*   From KCL at node $X$: $I_{D2} = I_{in}$. This sets $V_{out} = V_{TH2} + \sqrt{\frac{2I_{in}}{k'_2(W/L)_2}}$.
*   From KCL at node $V_{out}$: $I_{D1} = \frac{V_{DD} - V_{out}}{R_{D1}}$. This sets $V_X = V_{TH1} + \sqrt{\frac{2I_{D1}}{k'_1(W/L)_1}}$.
*   Any small perturbation (noise) will drive the circuit away from this point towards one of the two stable states described above.

### Summary
The circuit is a **bistable latch** (or Schmitt trigger) formed by cross-coupling two inverting stages.
*   It converts the input current $I_{in}$ and circuit parameters into a digital output $V_{out}$ (either High or Low).
*   A large $I_{in}$ tends to drive the circuit to State 2 ($V_{out}$ Low) by charging node $X$.
*   A small $I_{in}$ allows the circuit to settle in State 1 ($V_{out}$ High).

Because of the positive feedback, the circuit has two stable operating points (states):

Based on the provided circuit diagram, here is an analysis of its topology, operation, and function.

### 1. Circuit Components and Topology
The circuit consists of the following components:
*   **$M_1$ and $M_2$**: Two NMOS transistors.
*   **$R_{D1}$**: A load resistor connected to the supply voltage $V_{DD}$.
*   **$I_{in}$**: An input DC current source.
*   **$V_{DD}$**: The positive power supply.

**Connections:**
*   **Stage 1 ($M_1$):** Transistor $M_1$ is configured as a **Common-Source amplifier**. Its gate is connected to node **X**, its source is grounded, and its drain is connected to the output node **$V_{out}$** (via resistor $R_{D1}$). This stage acts as an inverter: a high voltage at X turns $M_1$ on, pulling $V_{out}$ low.
*   **Stage 2 ($M_2$):** Transistor $M_2$ is also configured as a Common-Source stage. Its gate is connected to **$V_{out}$**, its source is grounded, and its drain is connected to node **X**. The current source $I_{in}$ is connected to node X, acting as an active load or input driver. This stage also acts as an inverter: a high voltage at $V_{out}$ turns $M_2$ on, pulling node X low.

### 2. Feedback Analysis
The circuit forms a closed loop:
1.  The output **$V_{out}$** is fed to the gate of **$M_2$**.
2.  The drain of **$M_2$** (node **X**) is fed to the gate of **$M_1$**.
3.  The drain of **$M_1$** is the output **$V_{out}$**.

Since both stages ($M_1$ and $M_2$) are common-source amplifiers, each provides a $180^{\circ}$ phase shift (inversion).
*   Inversion 1: $V_{out} \rightarrow$ Node X (via $M_2$)
*   Inversion 2: Node X $\rightarrow V_{out}$ (via $M_1$)

Two inversions in a loop result in **Positive Feedback** ($180^{\circ} + 180^{\circ} = 360^{\circ}$).

### 3. Circuit Function: Bistable Latch / Schmitt Trigger
Due to the positive feedback, this circuit acts as a **bistable latch** or a **Schmitt trigger** (a comparator with hysteresis). It has two stable states and will regenerate any small difference to one of the rails.

The state of the circuit depends on the magnitude of the input current **$I_{in}$**.

**State 1: Low $I_{in}$ (Output High)**
*   If $I_{in}$ is small, the voltage at node **X** is low.
*   Since $V_X$ (Gate of $M_1$) is low, **$M_1$ is OFF**.
*   With $M_1$ off, no current flows through $R_{D1}$, so **$V_{out} \approx V_{DD}$** (High).
*   Since $V_{out}$ is High, the Gate of $M_2$ is High, turning **$M_2$ ON**.
*   $M_2$ conducts the current $I_{in}$ to ground. This is a consistent, stable state.

**State 2: High $I_{in}$ (Output Low)**
*   If $I_{in}$ is large, it forces the voltage at node **X** to rise (since it pushes current into the high-impedance gate of $M_1$ and the drain of $M_2$).
*   As $V_X$ rises, **$M_1$ turns ON**.
*   $M_1$ draws current through $R_{D1}$, causing **$V_{out}$ to drop**.
*   As $V_{out}$ drops, the Gate voltage of $M_2$ decreases, turning **$M_2$ OFF**.
*   With $M_2$ off, it can no longer sink the current $I_{in}$, causing $V_X$ to rise even further. This positive feedback loop drives $M_1$ fully ON and $M_2$ fully OFF.
*   Result: **$V_{out} \approx 0$** (Low) and **$V_X$ is High**.

### Summary
This circuit is a **current-controlled latch** or **regenerative comparator**.
*   It converts the analog input current $I_{in}$ into a digital output voltage $V_{out}$.
*   The positive feedback provides **hysteresis**, making the switching sharp and noise-immune.
*   **Low $I_{in}$** $\rightarrow$ $V_{out} = V_{DD}$ (Logic High).
*   **High $I_{in}$** $\rightarrow$ $V_{out} \approx 0$ (Logic Low).

## Circuit identification

The schematic contains two nMOS transistors whose **gate of each is tied to the drain of the other** (a cross‑coupled pair):

* **M1** – gate = node *X*, source = gnd, drain = *V*out (top node, also across *R*D1 to *V*DD).
* **M2** – gate = *V*out, source = gnd, drain = node *X*.
* A current source *I*in injects current into node *X*.

So node *X* is connected to {top of *I*in, gate of M1, drain of M2} and the output node is connected to {bottom of *R*D1, drain of M1, gate of M2, *V*out}.

## DC operating point

**Node X (KCL).** The gate of M1 draws no current, so all of *I*in must flow through M2:

$$I_{D2} = I_{in}$$

**M2 (saturation).** With source at gnd, $V_{GS2}=V_{out}$. Hence

$$I_{in}=\tfrac{\beta_2}{2}(V_{out}-V_{th2})^2 \;\Rightarrow\; \boxed{V_{out}=V_{th2}+\sqrt{\tfrac{2I_{in}}{\beta_2}}}$$

where $\beta_n=\mu_n C_{ox}(W/L)_n$. This is the central result: **the output voltage equals the gate‑source voltage M2 needs to carry $I_{in}$** – i.e. M2 acts as the current‑to‑voltage element.

**Output node (KCL).** The same current that leaves M1's drain comes from *R*D1:

$$I_{D1}=\frac{V_{DD}-V_{out}}{R_{D1}}$$

**M1 (saturation).** $V_{GS1}=V_X$, so

$$V_X = V_{th1}+\sqrt{\tfrac{2I_{D1}}{\beta_1}} = V_{th1}+\sqrt{\frac{2(V_{DD}-V_{out})}{\beta_1 R_{D1}^2}}$$

**Headroom / saturation conditions** for the intended region:

* M2 in saturation: $V_X \ge V_{OV2}=\sqrt{2I_{in}/\beta_2}$
* M1 in saturation: $V_{out} \ge V_{OV1}=\sqrt{2I_{D1}/\beta_1}$
* $0<V_{out}<V_{DD}$ (so $I_{D1}>0$).

Note that *M1* and *R*D1 do **not** set $V_{out}$; they only set $V_X$ and provide the bias path from *V*DD. The gain is essentially independent of $R_{D1}$ and of M1's size.

## Small‑signal (transresistance) analysis

Let $g_{m1},g_{m2}$ be the transconductances (with $I_{D2}=I_{in}$, $g_{m2}=\sqrt{2\beta_2 I_{in}}$), and include output conductances $g_{o1}=1/r_{o1},\,g_{o2}=1/r_{o2}$ and $g_R=1/R_{D1}$.

* Node X: $i_{in}=g_{m2}\,v_{out}+v_x/r_{o2}$
* Node $V_{out}$: $0=v_{out}(g_R+g_{o1})+g_{m1}\,v_x$

Eliminating $v_x$:

$$\boxed{\frac{v_{out}}{i_{in}}=\frac{1}{\,g_{m2}-\dfrac{g_R+g_{o1}}{g_{m1}\,r_{o2}\,}} \;\approx\; \frac{1}{g_{m2}}\left(1+\frac{g_R+g_{o1}}{g_{m1}g_{m2}r_{o2}}\right)}$$

So, to first order, the circuit is a **current‑to‑voltage (transresistance) converter** with

$$R_T \equiv \frac{dV_{out}}{dI_{in}} \approx \frac{1}{g_{m2}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\beta_2 I_{in}}}$$

## Feedback nature

The cross‑coupling (M1 gate←M2 drain, M2 gate←M1 drain) closes a **positive‑feedback** loop. The return ratio is

$$A_F=\frac{g_R+g_{o1}}{g_{m1}\,g_{m2}\,r_{o2}}$$

which multiplies the open‑loop $1/g_{m2}$ by $1/(1-A_F)$, i.e. it *boosts* the transresistance slightly. The intended (both‑saturation) operating point is the stable one only while $A_F<1$; if dimensions/bias make $A_F\to1$, the regenerative pair latches (the $V_{out}$ node exhibits negative differential resistance). With ideal transistors ($r_o\to\infty$) the feedback term vanishes and $v_{out}=i_{in}/g_{m2}$ exactly.

## Summary

* $I_{in}$ is forced through M2, and because M2's gate is at the output, $V_{out}=V_{GS2}(I_{in})=V_{th2}+\sqrt{2I_{in}/\beta_2}$.
* The differential transresistance is $\approx 1/g_{m2}$, set by M2 only; M1 and $R_{D1}$ set the bias voltage $V_X$ and the supply headroom.
* The gate–drain cross‑coupling gives a small positive‑feedback (regenerative) correction; the operating point is valid when both devices stay in saturation and $A_F<1$.

In short, the figure is a **cross‑coupled, positive‑feedback current‑to‑voltage converter** whose output tracks the gate‑source voltage of M2 required to pass $I_{in}$, with a small‑signal gain of about $1/g_{m2}$.

## 1. Reading the schematic

Both devices are **NMOS** (source arrow at the grounded terminal).

| Node | Connection |
|------|------------|
| $V_{out}$ | drain of $M_1$, gate of $M_2$, and one end of $R_{D1}$ |
| $X$ | gate of $M_1$, drain of $M_2$, top of $I_{in}$ |
| $M_1$ source, $M_2$ source | ground |
| $R_{D1}$ | $V_{DD}\rightarrow V_{out}$ |
| $I_{in}$ | ground $\rightarrow X$ (sources current *into* $X$) |

So $M_1$ and $M_2$ form a **cross‑coupled pair**: the drain of each is tied to the gate of the other. One drain carries a resistive load to $V_{DD}$, the other carries a current source to ground. The input is a current $I_{in}$, the output is $V_{out}$ → it is a **transresistance (I–V) circuit**.

## 2. DC operating point

Let $K_i=\tfrac12\mu C_{ox}(W/L)_i$ and assume both transistors are in saturation (checked below).

* $M_1$: $I_{D1}=K_1(V_X-V_{th1})^2$
* $M_2$: $V_{GS2}=V_{out}$, so $I_{D2}=K_2(V_{out}-V_{th2})^2$

KCL at $X$ (gate of $M_1$ draws no current) forces the entire current source through $M_2$:

$$I_{D2}=I_{in}\quad\Rightarrow\quad \boxed{V_{out}=V_{th2}+\sqrt{\frac{I_{in}}{K_2}}}$$

KCL at the $V_{out}$ node (gate of $M_2$ draws no current) gives the resistor current = $I_{D1}$:

$$\frac{V_{DD}-V_{out}}{R_{D1}}=K_1(V_X-V_{th1})^2\quad\Rightarrow\quad \boxed{V_X=V_{th1}+\sqrt{\frac{V_{DD}-V_{out}}{K_1 R_{D1}}}}$$

**Key observation:** $V_{out}$ is set *only* by $I_{in}$ and $M_2$; $M_1$ and $R_{D1}$ do **not** appear in it. Their only DC job is to fix the floating node $X$ (so that $M_2$'s $V_{DS}$ is large enough to keep it in saturation).

**Saturation conditions** (must be verified after solving):
$M_2$: $V_X\ge V_{out}-V_{th2}$ ; $M_1$: $V_{out}\ge V_X-V_{th1}$. Together these require $V_{out}-V_{th2}\le V_X\le V_{out}+V_{th1}$, which is satisfiable.

## 3. Small‑signal analysis

Let $v_x, v_{out}$ be the small‑signal voltages.

**Neglecting $r_o$ first.** $M_2$ gives $i_{in}=g_{m2}\,v_{out}$, while $M_1$'s drain equation only determines $v_x=-v_{out}/(g_{m1}R_{D1})$ and does not feed back into $i_{in}$. Hence

$$\boxed{\frac{v_{out}}{i_{in}}=\frac{1}{g_{m2}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{4K_2 I_{in}}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\mu C_{ox}(W/L)_2\,I_{in}}}}$$

The transresistance is set by $M_2$ alone; $M_1$ and $R_{D1}$ cancel out of the gain.

**Including $r_o$ (the important physics).** With $i_{in}$ injected,
$v_x=-v_{out}\big(R_{D1}\|r_{o1}\big)g_{m1}/1$ (from $M_1$), and $i_{in}=g_{m2}v_{out}+v_x/r_{o2}$, giving
$\dfrac{v_{out}}{i_{in}}=\dfrac{1}{\,g_{m2}-\dfrac{1/R_{D1}+1/r_{o1}}{g_{m1}r_{o2}}\,}$ — a slight increase over $1/g_{m2}$.

**Output resistance** (set $i_{in}=0$, apply $v_t$ at $V_{out}$): node $X$ sees only $M_2$'s drain, so $0=g_{m2}v_t+v_x/r_{o2}\Rightarrow v_x=-g_{m2}r_{o2}v_t$, and
$$R_{out}=\frac{v_t}{i_t}=\frac{1}{\dfrac{1}{R_{D1}}+\dfrac{1}{r_{o1}}-g_{m1}g_{m2}r_{o2}}$$

**Loop gain / stability.** Forward path $M_1$: $A=-g_{m1}(R_{D1}\|r_{o1})$. Return path $M_2$ (drain open): $\beta=v_x/v_{out}=-g_{m2}r_{o2}$. Thus
$$L=A\beta=+g_{m1}g_{m2}r_{o2}(R_{D1}\|r_{o1})>0$$
which is normally $\gg1$ (e.g. $g_m\!\sim\!0.5$ mS, $r_o\!\sim\!20$ k$\Omega$ gives $L\sim$ tens). The negative sign of the last term in $R_{out}$ confirms it: **$R_{out}<0$**.

## 4. Interpretation

* As a *DC* I–V converter the circuit works: $V_{out}=V_{th2}+\sqrt{I_{in}/K_2}$, a square‑law (diode‑like) transfer, with $M_1+R_{D1}$ biasing the internal node $X$ to hold $M_2$ in saturation.
* As a *small‑signal linear amplifier* the cross‑coupling is **positive feedback** ($L>1$), producing a **negative output resistance**. With the unavoidable parasitic capacitances at $X$ and $V_{out}$ this places a pole in the right‑half plane, so the biased operating point is **unstable**: the stage will latch to a rail or oscillate. In that sense the topology is a **regenerative (comparator/oscillator) circuit**, not a stable linear amplifier.

**Summary of element roles:** $I_{in}$ sets $V_{out}$ through the square‑law characteristic of $M_2$; $M_1$ with $R_{D1}$ is a self‑biasing network that fixes $V_X$ and, through the $r_o$ terms, closes a positive‑feedback loop that makes the linearized circuit regenerative (negative $R_{out}$).

## 1. What the circuit actually is

Reading the terminals carefully (both devices are NMOS, no inversion bubbles):

| Device | Gate | Drain | Source |
|--------|------|-------|--------|
| M₁ | node **X** | **V_out** | gnd |
| M₂ | node **V_out** | node **X** | gnd |

So the gate of each transistor is connected to the *drain* of the other, and the two drains carry a pull‑up (R_D1 at V_out) and a forced current (I_in at X). **M₁ and M₂ form a cross‑coupled pair.** M₁ is an inverter (X → V_out), M₂ is an inverter (V_out → X); two invators in a ring = **positive (regenerative) feedback** – i.e. a 2‑transistor latch / memory‑cell‑type circuit, not an ordinary linear amplifier.

Let k_i = ½ μ_n C_ox (W/L)_i, V_t the threshold, r_o_i = 1/(λ_i I_Di).

## 2. DC operating points

KCL (gate currents are zero):

* Node X:  **I_D2 = I_in**
* Node V_out:  **I_D1 = (V_DD − V_out)/R_D1**

**Point A – both in saturation** (the "mid‑point"):

$$V_{out}^{(A)} = V_t + \sqrt{I_{in}/k_2}$$
$$I_{D1}^{(A)} = \frac{V_{DD}-V_{out}^{(A)}}{R_{D1}},\qquad V_X^{(A)} = V_t + \sqrt{I_{D1}^{(A)}/k_1}$$

(valid while V_out ≥ V_X − V_t and V_X ≥ V_out − V_t).

**Point B – M₁ cut off, M₂ in triode** (the *stable* point, because the bias is asymmetric – I_in forces M₂ to conduct, so M₂ can never be off, whereas M₁ can):

$$V_{out}^{(B)} = V_{DD},\quad I_{D1}=0$$
$$V_X^{(B)} = (V_{DD}-V_t) - \sqrt{(V_{DD}-V_t)^2 - I_{in}/k_2}\;\;\approx\;\frac{I_{in}}{2k_2(V_{DD}-V_t)}\quad(\ll V_t)$$

(valid while V_X^{(B)} < V_t and I_in ≤ k_2(V_DD−V_t)²).

*Quick numeric check* (k₁=k₂=0.5 mA/V², V_t=0.5 V, V_DD=1.8 V, R_D1=10 kΩ, I_in=100 µA): Point A = (V_out, V_X)=(0.95 V, 0.91 V); Point B = (1.8 V, 0.08 V).

## 3. Small‑signal / feedback analysis

Let v_x, v_out be the ac signals at X and V_out (i_in = 0 for now).

* M₁: i_d1 = g_m1 v_x + v_out/r_o1
* M₂: i_d2 = g_m2 v_out + v_x/r_o2
* Node X: i_d2 = 0  ⇒  **v_x = −g_m2 r_o2 v_out**
* Node V_out: v_out/R_D1 + i_d1 = 0

Substituting:

$$v_{out}\left[\frac{1}{R_{D1}}+\frac{1}{r_{o1}}-g_{m1}g_{m2}r_{o2}\right]=0$$

A non‑zero v_out exists only when the **loop gain** equals 1:

$$\boxed{T = g_{m1}\,g_{m2}\,r_{o2}\,(R_{D1}\!\parallel\! r_{o1})}$$

The sign is **positive** (trace it: V_out↑ → M₂ wants more current → to keep I_in constant V_X must fall → M₁ wants less current → V_out rises further). At Point A, T ≫ 1 (with the numbers above T ≈ 10²), so the all‑saturation point is **unstable**.

**Output resistance** at V_out (inject a test current, i_in = 0):

$$R_{out}=\frac{1}{\frac{1}{R_{D1}}+\frac{1}{r_{o1}}-g_{m1}g_{m2}r_{o2}}=\frac{R_{D1}\!\parallel\! r_{o1}}{1-T}$$

* At Point A: T > 1 ⇒ **R_out < 0** (negative resistance – the algebraic signature of regeneration).
* At Point B: g_m1 = 0 ⇒ T = 0 ⇒ **R_out ≈ R_D1** (positive, stable).

**Transconductance** from a small modulation i_in to v_out (about Point A):

$$\frac{v_{out}}{i_{in}}=\frac{1}{g_{m2}\left(1-\tfrac{1}{T}\right)}$$

the denominator being reduced by the positive feedback (it would diverge as T→1).

## 4. Conclusion / function

The circuit is a **cross‑coupled, positive‑feedback (regenerative) NMOS pair** – the simplest MOS latch. The two transistors "fight" for the two nodes; the all‑on saturation solution is the **unstable switching threshold**, and the dynamics drive the circuit to a hard limit. Because the bias is asymmetric (resistive pull‑up on V_out, current‑source pull on X), there is only **one stable resting state: M₁ off, M₂ on, V_out ≈ V_DD and V_X ≈ I_in / [2k₂(V_DD−V_t)]** (a small voltage).
